en: The Treatise on the Refutation of Emptiness (*Kongkonglun*) to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Treatise composed by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of the Imperial Ming Dynasty. Jìmíng.
I prostrate to the three Prajñās of the true mark, Primordially free from the four extremes and the hundred negations;
To the Honored One who has fully cultivated and realized merit and wisdom, And whose nature and cultivation of compassion grant secret empowerment—
In order to treat those blind ones who perversely grasp at emptiness, And to proclaim the meaning of non-emptiness as it truly is.
"Amogha universally refutes all conceptual proliferation; because it accords with the *siddhānta*, it is called the *Śūnyatāvibhaṅga-śāstra*.
This is the homage and request for empowerment intended to state the purpose of composing this treatise and establishing its title.

"Prostrating" (*praṇipatya*) means bowing the head to the ground. Through sincere devotion of the mind, one moves the body and utters speech; this constitutes the diligent application of the three karmas.

This is an offering. As for the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): it is not a mark of existence, not a mark of non-existence, not a mark of neither existence nor non-existence, not a mark of neither non-existence nor non-non-existence, and not a mark of both existence and non-existence.
It is free from all marks, yet it universally serves as the mark for all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the "true mark. This true mark is the very essence of Prajñāpāramitā. Its essence is inherently quiescent and illuminating.
It is inconceivable. To illuminate in accordance with reality, wherein illumination is not different from quiescence, is called the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).
To express quiescence in accordance with reality, wherein the expression of quiescence is itself illumination, is called the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*).
Now, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the substance of both contemplative illumination and words. As for contemplative illumination, it illuminates the true mark; it illuminates words. As for...
As for "words" (or "letters"): they elucidate the true reality (*dharmatā*), and they elucidate contemplative insight (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). This one is not one; when one is raised, it is three.
These three are not three; when three are spoken, they are one.

Because it is intended to cause sentient beings to suddenly awaken to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, the true reality alone is raised to crown the three types of *prajñā*, since the essence of true reality governs all phenomena. This—
The true mark (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither both existent and non-existent, nor is it neither existent nor non-existent.
Because the true mark transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the contemplation of words and letters likewise transcends the four propositions.

Since the four propositions are transcended, the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*) are cut off, for those hundred negations do not, in total, go beyond the four propositions. These three dharmas of the true mark cannot...
It is inconceivable; it is neither cultivation nor realization, yet it is the foundation of all cultivation and realization. Those who have perfected cultivation and realization are the Tathāgatas.

They cultivate in accordance with the nature of reality and realize in accordance with the nature of reality. Since the principle of cause and effect is fully exhausted, there is nothing further to be added.

Regarding the cultivation and realization through differentiation: this refers to those bodhisattvas who fully cultivate their nature and fully realize their nature. It is like entering the great ocean, which becomes progressively deeper.
"Merit" (puṇya) is called the practice of merit; "wisdom" (prajñā) is called the practice of wisdom. Although the true mark (dharmatā) is not merit, it is the accumulation of all merits.
Cultivating conditions in accordance with the nature is the fulfillment of the merit of nature. Although the true mark is not wisdom, yet...

It is the root of all wisdom-practice and the true cultivation in accordance with the nature; this is the perfection of innate wisdom (*prakṛti-prajñā*). Relying upon words and letters, there is the merit of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*);
merit itself is the true mark, and thus one is fully endowed with both merit and wisdom. Relying upon contemplative observation, there is the wisdom of the true mark;
wisdom itself is the true mark, and thus one is fully endowed with both merit and wisdom. Since the essence of the true mark is venerable, for this reason—

Through the cultivation and realization of merit and wisdom, one becomes a Dvipada-agra (Two-legged Honored One). Furthermore, if true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) were not merit and wisdom, one would not be called "Honored";
for all sentient beings are already fully endowed with the essence of true reality. Likewise, if merit and wisdom were not true reality, they would also not be called "Honored";
for although all provisional and Hinayana practitioners may possess various forms of merit and wisdom, they do not achieve the Unsurpassed Great [Enlightenment].
Because of Bodhi, through the meaning of its inherent nature, wondrous cultivation is perfected; through the meaning of wondrous cultivation, the virtues of the nature are then manifested.
If one were to mention only the virtues of cultivation without mentioning the virtues of the nature, then sentient beings and Buddhas would be entirely separate and distinct.

Birth cannot evoke it, and the Buddha cannot respond to it. If one were to mention only the virtues of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*) without mentioning the virtues of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), then Buddhas and sentient beings would be of a single, equal flavor;
the Buddha would not be able to bestow anything, and sentient beings would have nothing to be bestowed upon.
Now, by means of the compassionate vows perfected through cultivation by all Buddhas within the nature of sentient beings, they empower the original sentient beings within the nature of all Buddhas.
Possessing cultivated virtue, one is able to uproot all suffering of conceptual proliferation and bestow the bliss of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Nature merges with nature; cultivation merges with cultivation; nature merges with cultivation; and cultivation merges with nature. Thus, nature and cultivation are non-dual.
The essence of the sentient being and the Buddha are identical; therefore, the meaning of bestowing empowerment is established.
Furthermore, for the practitioner, whether it be the body and bodily karma, the speech and vocal karma, or the mind and mental karma, their very substance is the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Because their very substance is the true reality, there is no distinction between the one who prostrates and the object of prostration. One must penetrate this nature of subject and object.
It is neither subject nor object, nor does it possess the nature of subject or object. It universally serves as the basis for all subjects and objects;
there is not a single subject or object that is not the entire reality (dharmatā) in its great essence and great function.
Therefore, the three karmas can become the "inducers," and the Buddhas can become the "induced. The Buddhas can become the "respondents," and the practitioners can become the "responded-to."
This is the intent of the homage and the request for [the Buddha’s] empowerment. Next, regarding the intent of composing this treatise and establishing its title: Question:
Since the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddhas and patriarchs above are already sufficient, why is it necessary to compose this treatise again? Answer:
It is for the purpose of treating those who are like the blind and who have wrongly grasped emptiness (*śūnyatā*). All sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom and are thus unable to see.

They do not know how to contemplate the true essence of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), nor do they understand its scriptural expression; they are like a group of blind men who cannot see the color of milk.
They form interpretations based merely on words: hearing of a crane, they say it moves; hearing of snow, they say it is cold, and so forth. Those who hear this sutra are just the same.
Although the original sutra destroys all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) to enable one to realize the ultimate reality, these blind people merely hear...

Having negated characteristics, they then cling to the absence of characteristics and become attached to emptiness, thereby forming erroneous views that destroy conventional truth and repudiate cause and effect.
For this reason, the Buddha said: "It would be better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness even as small as a mustard seed.
Yet such persons do not know the true nature of reality; although they have forever departed from all illusory fabrications, [they remain bound by their attachment].

Its marks and its essential nature are not empty. Because from time immemorial it has been eternal and unchanging, it is fully endowed with the functional power of inherent virtues exceeding the sands of the Ganges. It is not only adorned by the various myriad practices;

rather, the myriad practices it possesses are none other than those inherently complete and none other than those inherently arising. To cite even a single practice, there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*).
The total body and great function are without division or measure; they are mutually pervasive and mutually fused, for their essence is the Dharma-realm.

Such is the meaning. It is asked: "Does such a meaning not already thoroughly refute all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*)—namely, the proliferation of the view of existence, the proliferation of the view of emptiness, the proliferation of the view of both existence and emptiness, and the proliferation of the view of neither existence..."

It is not a frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) based on the view of emptiness; rather, it is the frivolous proliferation of the four single views, the four compound views, and the complete set of four views, explained at length up to one hundred and eight views. Among all such nets of views and frivolous proliferations, there is none that it does not utterly destroy.
Why, then, is it designated as "the refutation of emptiness"? The answer is: it is so named because it accords with the *siddhānta* (established tenet). It is called [the refutation of emptiness].
Refuting [the notion of] emptiness. There are four *siddhāntas*: first, the *loka-siddhānta*, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to attain joy;

second, the *pudgala-siddhānta*, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to produce roots of goodness; third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to extinguish craving and views;
fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to enter the profound.

This is for the sake of principle. Now, to treat the view of wrongly grasping emptiness (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*) is called "refuting emptiness," which accords with the meaning of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint).

Furthermore, within this therapeutic [standpoint], it still encompasses the four *siddhāntas*. That is to say, there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the discourse refuting emptiness, give rise to joy;
furthermore, there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness increase and whose attachment to views is extinguished, thereby attaining realization.
Entering into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Such various [explanations] serve different purposes. For these reasons, it is necessary to compose this treatise.
The essence of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is a supreme jewel;
its characteristics are indestructible, and its function is able to shatter all things, while its nature remains eternally as it is.
By analogy, the three aspects of *prajñā* are neither three nor not-three; both the specific and the general establish the *pāramitā*.
The Treatise says: This is the general title of this single scripture. In relation to other scriptures, it is called "specific";
in relation to the scriptural text itself, it is further called "general. Whether specific or general, that which is expounded is non-dual; therefore, it is said that both "establish the *pāramitā*."
It is the ultimate. "Vajra" is a metaphor; "Prajñāpāramitā" is the Dharma. Because it is the most adamantine among metals, it is called "vajra.
This treasure is precious and is used as a metaphor for the Prajñā of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the most honored among all dharmas.
Its characteristics are firm and solid; no thing can destroy it. This is used as a metaphor for the *prajñā* of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), which love and views cannot invade.
Its function is fierce and sharp, capable of shattering all things. This is used as a metaphor for the *prajñā* of words and letters (*nāma-prajñā*), which can sever all doubts. Furthermore:
Because the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is revered, the contemplation of letters is likewise revered;
because the contemplation is indestructible, it is the true reality wherein letters are indestructible. Because letters sever doubt, they are the true reality wherein contemplation severs doubt.
For example, because its substance is a supreme treasure, it cannot be destroyed by anything, yet it can destroy all things.
It is not destroyed by anything; therefore, it can destroy all things and is called the supreme treasure (*ratna*).

Because it can destroy all things, it is named the supreme treasure such that no object can destroy it. The single essence (*tattva*) and the three meanings (*artha*) become more distinct when blended together;
the three meanings and the single essence become more unified when differentiated. The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is eternally abiding as the essence; this essence is itself the Dharma.
The body takes contemplation that accords with principle as its essence; this essence is *prajñā*. It takes the severing of doubt through words as its function;
this function is *vimukti*. These three dharmas together constitute the name, and these three meanings serve as the metaphors. These three meanings are eternally so by nature:
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot cause them to increase, and all sentient beings cannot cause them to decrease.
It is neither awakening nor delusion; it is neither "that" nor "this. Because it does not belong to either delusion or awakening, it serves as the universal basis for both delusion and awakening.
Because its nature is devoid of "that" and "this," by relying upon it, one becomes "that" and becomes "this. In Sanskrit, this is called *pāramitā*;
here it is translated as "reaching the other shore," and also as "the Infinite Crossing. To be deluded regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) constitutes the path of suffering.
Delusion regarding contemplation becomes affliction; delusion regarding liberation becomes fetters and karma.
Therefore, that which is not this is described as this, and is called the boundless ocean of birth and death. Awakening to the path of suffering is the Dharma-body;
awakening to afflictions is contemplation; awakening to fetters and karma is liberation. Therefore, that which is not that is described as that, and is called the Perfection (Pāramitā).

This prajñā is not the pāramitā; rather, it is the various forms of wisdom that resemble it.
Thirdly, this prajñā is the pāramitā—namely, the three types of prajñā revealed in this sutra.
There is no further statement such as "this is a pāramitā but not prajñā," because if the five perfections were devoid of prajñā, they could not reach the other shore. As for the five perfections...

Because all that reaches the other shore is named *prajñā*, it is for this reason that the teaching of *prajñā* alone constitutes the complete exposition of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*).

One should know that these six perfections and myriad practices are all like a vajra: they transcend linguistic expression and are free from conceptualization, yet they are not a state of annihilation.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is without sound or letters, And is devoid of time, place, principal, or retinue;
Yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, it turns the wheel of Dharma, Being established through the six modes of proof to inspire conviction.
The treatise states: The essence of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is called the ultimate truth. It is neither the subject that believes nor the object that is believed. It is not...

It can be heard, yet it is not that which is heard; it is not subsumed within the three periods of time, nor is it contained within spatial directions. It is neither subject nor companion, neither one nor many.

Yet the capacity to hear and that which is heard, as well as time and place, subject and companion, and unity and multiplicity—all are accomplished by relying upon the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, if one knows that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is not manifold, then all that is manifold is none other than the ultimate truth.

As for the single ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is to penetrate the true nature (*dharmatā*) without destroying conventional designations (*prajñapti*). One may thus enter this sutra through faith;
this constitutes the specific introduction (*nidāna*) as distinguished from the general introduction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, at the hour of eating, put on his robes and took up his bowl, entering the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having completed his alms-round through the city in due order, he returned to his original location. When he had finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and sat down upon a prepared seat.
In eating, clothing, walking, and sitting, all activities are the principle itself; All *vinaya* precepts are the practice of the Buddha.
Within each and every action, one perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*). One should understand that this is the protection, mindfulness, and entrustment [of the Buddhas].
The treatise says: At the beginning of the final age, when those who aspire toward the Mahāyāna and study the profound *prajñā* first encounter these matters, they tend to treat them with contempt.

Regarding the detailed practices of the *vinaya*, you have repeatedly claimed that the Great Way does not restrict itself to minor details and that a great elephant does not follow the tracks of a rabbit.
Yet, how can you fail to consider that the Tathāgata, the Great Sage and King of the Dharma, donned robes, carried an alms bowl, begged for food, and sat in the lotus posture?

In every single detail, they were entirely consistent with the dignified deportment of a bhikṣu; there was never even the slightest deviation. Thus we know that the phenomenal fact is itself the principle.

If one wishes to discard the three robes of dyed cloth while merely speaking in the air of the robes of shame, modesty, and patience, why not simultaneously abolish the six flavors of the human world and instead speak in the air of the flavor of Dharma-joy and the bliss of dhyāna? Formerly, Chan Master Gaofeng Miao...
In his room, the Master posed a question, saying: "A great practitioner of the Way should follow the conduct of the Buddha. Why, then, do you not observe the *vinaya*?
One must know that all *vinaya* rules are none other than the conduct of the Buddha; how can they be called mere rabbit-tracks or minor details?
Since you do not follow the conduct of the Buddha, how can you be called a great practitioner of the Way? You must realize that even in the single act of putting on a robe, it is already complete."
The garment of shame, remorse, and the merit of patience; a single meal that provides the sustenance of dhyāna-joy and the joy of the Dharma, transcending the world;
a single act of begging that reveals the Tathāgata’s practice of compassion; and a single cross-legged sitting.
One then knows that the Tathāgata sits upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas; therefore, every single door of practice is none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*).

This enables bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature to see all Tathāgatas as their own companions in practice, whereby they realize the true mark—this is called "skillfully protecting and mindful of them.
It causes bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature to rely upon this Dharma and Vinaya, dwelling correctly and increasing therein, so that they may advance toward the true mark.
This is called "the excellent entrustment. For this reason, it is titled the "Introductory Chapter on the Arousing [of the Resolve].

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, being amidst the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all..."

“Bodhisattva, you have entrusted the bodhisattvas well. World-Honored One, how should a son or daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dwell? How should they subdue their minds?”
Realizing the ultimate and provisionally employing skillful means, he skillfully discerns the capacities [of beings].
Because of his protective mindfulness and entrustment, it is rare that one should resolve to generate the mind [of awakening], abide in the mind of subduing, and correspond with *prajñā*.
Regarding this, the treatise says: For three reasons, it is praised as rare. The *prajñā* of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is difficult to realize and difficult to enter; only...
The Buddha has reached the ultimate depth; therefore, he is rare and marvelous. Having already realized true wisdom (*jñāna*), he bestows expedient means (*upāya*) upon sentient beings.

Since the provisional and the real are non-dual, he is rare and marvelous. Knowing that among the various capacities of beings some are mature and others are not, he protects and mindfully guards those who are mature, while entrusting those who are not yet mature.
At all times and within all practices, he possesses these two benefits; therefore, he is rare and marvelous. Anuttara...
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment";

it is the fruit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). The "arousing of the mind" (*cittotpāda*) is the supreme resolve that proceeds from cause toward this fruit. It is the *prajñā* that enters into the principle.
It is called "abiding. How should one abide? This asks about the fruit of abiding. "How does one subdue the mind? This asks about the cause of purification.
Now, although unsurpassed bodhi is termed a "fruit," its essence is not a fruit. One gives rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Although it is called a cause, its essence is not a cause; it is neither effect nor cause—the precious *dharmakāya* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
One should abide in this contemplation-observation; this is the indestructible principle. To subdue [delusions] is liberation; to sever afflictions is its function.
Therefore, it is named the "Inquiry Corresponding to Prajñā."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you:
how sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide and how they should subdue their minds."
"It is so, World-Honored One. We wish most earnestly to hear it.
Because it accords with the principle and accords with the capacity [of the listener], it is excellent and excellent.

Regarding the statement that one possesses the wisdom of hearing and should contemplate with truth and application, there are cases where something accords with the principle but does not accord with the capacity. For example, when the Great Dharma is preached, those of small capacity are unable to endure it.
There may be that which accords with the occasion but does not accord with principle, such as when it is said that worldly goodness does not lead out of birth and death.

Speaking exhaustively according to principle, if something does not accord with principle, it certainly cannot accord with the occasion; for principle is neither provisional nor ultimate, yet it is capable of being both provisional and ultimate.

Both the provisional and the ultimate are principle, for they are like sweet and bitter medicines, both of which are medicinal. If something does not accord with the capacity [of the listener], it certainly does not accord with principle;

for a teaching that is inappropriate to the capacity becomes a non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). Just as medicine has no distinction between noble and base, it is effective only when it cures the illness.
One who possesses the perfection of wisdom derived from hearing: if there is hearing but no wisdom, it is like having a lamp but no eyes—one does not see the true nature of reality.
If there is wisdom but no hearing, it is like sitting in a dark room—one likewise does not see the true nature of reality.
He is thus exhorted to listen attentively, so as to perfect the wisdom derived from hearing, and to give rise to the wisdom derived from reflection and the wisdom derived from cultivation.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way:
'Whatever kinds of sentient beings there may be—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all to [attain...]"

He enters parinirvāṇa and brings them to extinction. In this way, he brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinction, yet in reality, there is no sentient being who attains extinction.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva.
Vast, foremost, and ever-unerring— The four minds are likewise the three dedications.
With such vows, one skillfully subdues the mind, Able to unify the single mind and the three *prajñās*.
The Treatise says: "The vast mind" is also called the boundless mind; it refers to the pervasiveness of its objective sphere, which is horizontal (*tiryak*).

It extends horizontally across the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and vertically through the three realms (*tridhātu*). The four modes of birth constitute that which dwells, while the three realms constitute the place wherein they dwell.

That which is born from an egg shell is called "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*), such as fish, birds, and the like. That which is contained within a womb is called "womb-born" (*jarāyuja*), such as humans, domestic animals, and the like.

That which arises by means of moisture is called "moisture-born" (*saṃsvedaja*), such as insects, ants, and the like. That which appears instantaneously is called "transformation-born" (*upapāduka*), such as the various devas and the like. As for those with form, [they belong to] the desire realm...

The two realms of form and the formless realm consist of the four heavens beginning with the Sphere of Infinite Space. Among these four spheres of emptiness, the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness are called "possessing perception.
The Sphere of Nothingness is called "non-perception. The beings in the Peak of Existence are called "neither possessing perception nor non-perception.
The first mind is also called the supreme mind; that is to say, "I shall cause all to enter nirvana without remainder."
...and through this, one attains parinirvāṇa. This is not the *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna.
The *Guṇapradāna-bodhisattva-śāstra* asks: "What is the meaning of *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*? It refers to the realization that all phenomena are unborn and empty by nature;
the eternal cessation of all afflicted aggregates (*skandha*); and the perfection of pure physical marks and boundless, marvelous qualities for the benefit of others."
Adorned and extensively benefiting all sentient beings, his wondrous deeds are inexhaustible. The Tiantai Commentary states:

"In the Mahāyāna, there are no afflictions that are not exhausted, no virtues that are not perfected, and no names that remain unexhausted. Regarding the "constant mind," it is also called the "mind embraced by love. As the Sūtra says:
"Thus I have brought immeasurable sentient beings to *nirvāṇa*, yet in reality, there are no sentient beings who have attained *nirvāṇa*. The Śāstra states:
The Bodhisattva loves all sentient beings as if they were himself; when sentient beings attain liberation, they are none other than himself.
This is called "embracing through love. Now, regarding this scriptural passage, it should be interpreted according to the treatise:
although all sentient beings are infinite in number, they are collectively not apart from the mind-nature that is identical to one's own. Therefore, this is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Sentient beings, you must know that in reality there are no sentient beings outside of the mind who attain extinction. It is not that the self-nature of sentient beings does not attain extinction;
rather, it is to cause them to realize the bliss of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Indeed, the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally the realm of Great Nirvana.
Due to delusion and ignorance, birth and death are vast and boundless, like a person with cataracts who falsely perceives flowers in the sky.
Now, to awaken to the fact that the fundamental is extinction is itself called "crossing over. It is not that there is a "this shore" to be abandoned, nor is there a "far shore" to be reached.
If one does not realize that all sentient beings are identical to the nature of my own mind, then the notions of "other" and "self" will arise, and one will be unable to embrace them with love.
If one does not realize that the essence of all birth and death is itself nirvana, then [the notion of] difficulty will arise.
The mind of deliverance cannot exhaustively practice the bodhisattva path until the end of the future; therefore, in reality, there are no words for it.
This is to negate the external calculation that sentient beings exist and to negate the internal calculation that birth and death are real dharmas within the mind.
It does not mean that one does not vow to deliver those sentient beings who are like illusions, which are one's own mind. A non-perverted mind is also called the mind of right wisdom.

The Sūtra says: "If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self and so forth, he is not a bodhisattva. These four marks (*catur-nimitta*) are inverted minds. To have them is called "not [a bodhisattva]," and to lack them is called "is [a bodhisattva]";

this is because one attains the realization by abandoning the delusion. That which acts as a master is called the "self" (*ātman*); that which possesses physical form is called a "person" (*pudgala*);
the harmony of various conditions is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*); and the continuous succession of similar states is called a "life-sustainer" (*jīvin*). These are the sixteen [aspects].
The four aspects of knowledge and vision are briefly cited here to reveal the false attachments of the *pudgala*. If these attachments are absent, one is said to have attained right knowledge.
The "four minds" are also the three types of dedication; they refer to the three kinds of dedication cultivated by a bodhisattva.
This means turning oneself toward others, turning causes toward the fruit, and turning phenomena toward principle. Here, the "vast mind" signifies the meaning of turning oneself toward others;
the "foremost mind" signifies the meaning of turning causes toward the fruit; and the "constant mind" and "non-perverted mind" [signify the remaining aspects].
This means turning phenomena toward principle. By means of this vow, one skillfully subdues the mind so that the cause becomes pure;

thus, one realizes the nature of the three kinds of prajñā within the single mind. Turning oneself toward others, one realizes the nature of liberation—this is likened to being able to destroy all things.
Turning the cause toward the fruit, one realizes the nature of contemplative observation—this is likened to being indestructible by anything. Turning phenomena toward...
The Principle: It accords with the nature of the Dharmakāya; it is like a physical body that is itself a supreme treasure.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without abiding in anything. That is to say, one should not abide in form when practicing giving;
one should not abide in sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should act thus...
This giving does not dwell upon signs. Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling upon signs, that merit and virtue is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the empty space in the eastern direction be measured or conceived?
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving without abiding in signs is likewise immeasurable.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed."

To dwell nowhere is the true dwelling; the means of livelihood, fearlessness, and the Dharma are subsumed within the three *dānas* (giving), which fulfill the six *pāramitās* (perfections) through the sequence of one, two, and three. To dwell like space is what is taught.

The commentary states: Regarding the previous questions and the granting of permission, all involve first abiding and subsequently descending; this arises from ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) giving rise to expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*).
Furthermore, in the present response, the sequence of first descending and then abiding refers to entering into ultimate wisdom from provisional wisdom.
By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one abides within prajñā, fervently practicing the six pāramitās without grasping at signs.

Therefore, it can cause even a small gift to become equal to space. There are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material resources (*āmiṣadāna*), which is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*);
second, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), which consists of the two perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*);

third, the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*), which consists of the three perfections of diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). One who does not dwell in the six sense-objects [practices these].
One does not cling to its cause, nor does one grasp at its fruit. To not cling to the cause means not perceiving a self as the giver, another as the recipient, or an object as that which is given;
for whether it be the self, the person, or the object, these causal conditions lack intrinsic nature.

Because they are like illusions and dreams, they are manifestations of the mind alone; because they take the mind as their cause, they constitute its substance, and that substance is the *dharmadhātu*.
"Not grasping at results" means not seeking future retributions such as superior forms and so forth.
"Not dwelling on signs" means that signs are merely the six sense-objects, whether causes or results—namely, all that currently manifests before one, the wondrous [perfections].

All practices are fundamentally constituted by the entirety of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Therefore, whichever single practice one undertakes, its fundamental nature is the entire body and great function of the true mark.
It is like taking up the ocean to form a bubble, or taking up a bubble to encompass the ocean.

Yet, because sentient beings dwell within appearances, they falsely calculate effects and causes, and perceive the large as small. If one can abide in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), [then all is resolved].
It does not abide in any marks. For example, the space within a mustard seed and the space of the ten directions are non-dual and indistinguishable in nature.
This is because space is neither internal nor external, neither this nor that, nor any cardinal direction, nor possesses any form or characteristic; there is no small space distinct from great space.
The merit of signlessness is truly great; it does not mean that there is no merit. Not abiding in the signs of defilement is called "abiding according to the teaching";
it is not that there is no proper abiding. Therefore, one skillfully refutes the evil view of grasping at emptiness.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there may be, they are all empty and false. If one sees that all marks are non-marks..."
These are the hundred Tathāgatas.
The fruit and virtue of the Tathāgata are inconceivable; his physical marks are non-marks, which is the true mark (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*).
While not departing from all marks, they are explained as non-marks. Thus should one perceive the three bodies of the Buddha.
The Commentary states: According to other treatises, from this point onward, all [sections] consist of questions and answers intended to dispel doubts.

Fearing that there might be doubt as to how the marks of merit (lakṣaṇa) are achieved at the time of fruition when a Bodhisattva practices giving while not dwelling on signs (animitta), he asks in anticipation:
"Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? The Venerable One has already realized the true principle of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
He immediately replied: "One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of physical characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Why is this?

The physical characteristics spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical characteristics. This is because the true mark (*dharmatā*) remains unchanging while following conditions; thus it is described as 'physical characteristics. Yet, as it follows conditions without changing, it is 'not physical characteristics.
This [realization] constitutes the awakening that the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* are not the ultimate reality, yet they do not depart from the ultimate reality."
The Buddha welcomed his understanding and expanded upon it, saying: "All that possesses marks is entirely illusory and false.

It is not only the marks of the retributive and transformational bodies, produced through cultivated virtue, that are called illusory and false; even the marks of the Dharma-body’s inherent virtue are likewise so."

This, too, is false and illusory. If one sees that all marks are non-marks—just as realizing that a wave is entirely water with no separate mark of "wave," or that a bubble is entirely the sea with no separate mark of "bubble"—then one will not separately grasp at the marks of the Reward or Transformation bodies outside the Dharma-body, nor will one separately grasp at the marks of the Dharma-body outside the Reward and Transformation bodies;
rather, every single thing and every single phenomenon is [the Dharma-body].
The Tathāgata is the single essence of the three bodies (trikāya).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these,"
“Do they give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhūti, “Do not speak thus.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who are able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as the truth.
You should know that such persons have planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas alone, but have already [planted them] under countless Buddhas.”

Subhūti, those who have planted roots of goodness under millions of Buddhas, and upon hearing these phrases, give rise to even a single thought of pure faith—in all such beings, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that they shall obtain such immeasurable merit. Why is this?
Because these beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a being, or the notion of a life-span.

There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas. Why is this? If these sentient beings take up marks with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If they take up the mark of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
Why is this? If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma, one is immediately attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
For this reason, one should neither grasp at the Dharma nor grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this very reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said:
"O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
"Maintaining the precepts, cultivating merit, and possessing wisdom—because the roots of goodness are deep, one's merit and virtue are vast.
This is seen by the Buddha-eye and known by the Buddha-wisdom; it transcends the attachment to self and dharmas and crosses over to the other shore.
The Commentary says: Giving without dwelling on signs (*animitta*) is the cause of purity. The non-existence of all signs (*alakṣaṇa*) is the fruit of purity. It transcends...
When one’s mind is detached from views, who could believe and rejoice? Because the Venerable One had thus fallen into doubt, the Buddha answered and explained, saying, "Do not speak thus.
These words are of an indefinite nature. If one lacks the three roots of goodness, although one may live in the time of a Buddha, true faith will not arise.
If one possesses the three roots of goodness, even at a later time, one can give rise to pure faith. [The three roots of goodness...]
Regarding the "roots": first, upholding the precepts; second, cultivating merit; third, possessing wisdom. First, as for upholding the precepts:

Guṇadatta says that because one beheld immeasurable Buddhas in past lives and made offerings to them all, there are three kinds of such offerings: first, attending to them at their side; second, providing whatever is required;
and third, inquiring after and receiving the essential points of the Dharma. Because one is able to protect [the teachings], it is called [upholding the precepts].
It is called *śīla* (ethical discipline). This means being able to skillfully guard the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). That, moreover, has three aspects:

first, *śīla* as abstention, because it involves abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action; second, *śīla* as performance, because it involves performing the actions that constitute the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
third, *śīla* as progression, because it leads toward the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Second, regarding those who cultivate merit (*puṇya*): this refers to their virtuous qualities.
The Cloud of Giving says: Because one plants the three roots of goodness, such as non-attachment; because of being upright, gentle, and possessing wisdom and compassion;
and because those with wisdom understand that both birth and dharmas are empty. To know the emptiness of birth is to realize the absence of marks such as self or person.
To know the emptiness of dharmas is to realize the absence of the mark of dharmas, as well as the absence of the mark of non-dharmas. Although...
It is said that the two emptinesses are but a single principle. If one does not grasp, then both self and phenomena are fundamentally empty;
yet if one grasps even once, both become attachments. Regarding these three roots of goodness: the former do not include the latter, while the latter must necessarily possess the former.

The former two serve as auxiliaries, and the latter one serves as the primary. Without correct faith, the auxiliary wholesome merits will be slight; without auxiliary goodness, there can be no correct faith.
It does not arise because its roots are deep; thus, its merit is immeasurable. This is known by the Buddha’s wisdom through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), not through inference.
It is seen by the Buddha-eye, which illuminates and exhaustively penetrates cause and effect, and is not the fleshly eye.

In the world, there are those who boast about the signless (*animitta*) while casting aside moral discipline (*śīla*) and merit as if they were unheard of, falsely claiming that one should not cling to the characteristics of the precepts.
One knows that [the practitioner] has entirely fallen into the characteristics of broken precepts, yet falsely claims not to be attached to the characteristics of merit.

One does not know that [the practitioner] has entirely fallen into the characteristics of manifold transgressions. For this reason, the Tathāgata earnestly and solemnly issues this specific admonition. Why is this?

If one grasps at the characteristics of what is non-Dharma, one is immediately attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. This is because ordinary beings have not yet attained realization regarding the nature of the precepts.

Merit. Its very substance is formlessness (*animitta*). Yet, if one seeks the merit of the precepts of formlessness separately, one does not realize that by rejecting the dharmic characteristics of the precepts and their merit, one immediately falls into the characteristics of non-dharmas (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Having grasped what is non-dharmic, attachment arises in full force.

If one wishes to realize the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), one will go further and further astray. Therefore it is said: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas. This is as the Buddha taught.
As stated by the Venerable [Dharmarakṣa]: "If one has not yet even attained non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust, how could one further follow after the affairs of killing, stealing, and lust?

Unrighteous characteristics (adharma-lakṣaṇa) are like a disease, and righteous characteristics (dharma-lakṣaṇa) are like medicine. When the disease is exhausted, the medicine is discarded; why would one take up the disease again?

Unrighteous characteristics are like this shore, and righteous characteristics are like a raft. Once one has crossed to the other shore, one abandons even the raft; how much less would one [cling to it]?"

While performing activities on this shore, if one has not yet reached the other shore, one should simply resolutely abandon the non-Dharma of this shore, but must never hastily discard the raft of Dharma-characteristics.
If one has already reached the other shore and returns to deliver sentient beings, one need only employ the raft of Dharma-characteristics;
there is no further need for the non-Dharma of this shore. Alternatively, one may manifest as a warning upon this shore.
[These cases], such as Vāsavadatta and so forth, shall be discussed separately. However, for the practitioner today, it is fortunate that they should examine their own hearts.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has preached, there is no fixed dharma called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. Why is this?
All dharmas preached by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and inexpressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas."
The Dharma. Why is this? All noble and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If the Dharma were obtainable or expressible, it would be conditioned and not the true meaning;
what is spoken would not be without causes and conditions, but would instead accord with the realization of the noble and holy ones' unconditioned state.
The meaning of the distinctions among the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should be understood, as in the analogy of the fathom, the cubit, and space.
The treatise says: "Furthermore, when crossing to the other shore, both dharma and non-dharma are abandoned. How then did the World-Honored One attain the dharmas of enlightenment?
Is there anything he has taught? This question is posed in order to dispel such doubts. The Venerable One [Vasubandhu] profoundly grasps this.
This is the Buddha’s intention; therefore, he replied accordingly: "Unsurpassed Bodhi transcends emotion and is free from views; it is the ultimate shore.
Not only is there no mark of non-dharma, but even a mark of dharma cannot be found. Thus it is said: 'There is no fixed dharma named unsurpassed Bodhi.
Since that which is realized transcends emotion and is free from views, that which is taught likewise transcends emotion and is free from views."
Therefore, it is said that there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. Why is this?

Although the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) lies beyond the path of language and the sphere where mental activity ceases—such that it cannot be grasped or expressed—the Tathāgata may nevertheless speak of it by means of the four *siddhāntas*.
However, the dharma he preaches does so because it accords with these four *siddhāntas*.
Therefore, not a single word or phrase fails to transcend emotion and leave behind views; it leaves behind faults and cuts off all that is non-true.
Thus, all are neither graspable nor expressible, neither the Dharma nor non-Dharma.

Indeed, not only is that which the Tathāgata realized and taught beyond emotion and free from views, leaving behind faults and cutting off all that is non-true, but even that which all worthies and sages have realized is likewise so.
It transcends emotion and is free from views; it is devoid of faults and cuts off all that is non-virtuous. This is because all worthies and sages alike enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.
Since it is called "unconditioned," how can there be distinctions? One must know that the unconditioned has no distinctions, yet distinctions do not exist apart from the unconditioned.
It is like empty space, which is not measured by the *zhang* or *chi*, yet the *zhang* and *chi* reveal empty space. It is also like entering the ocean gradually...
Next, it becomes increasingly profound. The ocean is neither deep nor shallow; both the shallow and the deep are the ocean.

To claim that there are distinctions within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma would mean one has not severed ignorance. How can you cling to the nature (*prakṛti*) while subverting cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and yet grant [the existence of the six] while simultaneously refusing them?

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? This merit is not a nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who receives, upholds, and even recites as few as four lines of verse from this sutra and explains them for others, their merit shall surpass that [previous merit].
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because all Buddhas and the unsurpassed...
The Dharma of *samyak-saṃbodhi* all issues from this sutra. Subhūti, that which is called the Buddha-Dharma is precisely not the Buddha-Dharma.
The perfection of the gift of Dharma possesses two adornments; one should know that the gift of material wealth is not superior because it is not the cause [of liberation].
The gift of Dharma is free from grasping and attachment; grasping and attachment are not called "upholding. The treatise says:
This uses the merit of the gift of material wealth as a comparison for the gift of Dharma. Although the gift of material wealth may be great, [it does not equal the gift of Dharma].

Among the three types of giving (*dāna*), this belongs solely to the giving of material goods (*āmiṣadāna*). Now, to be able to receive and uphold [this teaching] and explain it for others, one must possess the three kinds of roots of goodness as previously explained;
one should know that this constitutes the fulfillment of the two adornments (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*).
Furthermore, if the gift of wealth is not guided by Prajñā, then those who cultivate such deluded merit are called "enemies of the third world," because...
It increases birth and death, remaining unmoving and not emerging; therefore, it is said that this is precisely the nature of non-merit.

This is merely speaking of "much" in contrast to "little," yet "much" is still finite. The gift of Dharma gives rise to the merit of the fruit of Buddhahood; it is the cause for transcending the world.

The merit thereof is supreme. Having made this comparative assessment, he further feared that those in the final age might produce interpretations based merely on the words and become biasedly attached to this sutra, thinking that this alone constitutes the Buddha-dharma and that no further merits need be cultivated. Therefore, he spoke again, saying:
"That which is called the Buddha-dharma is not the Buddha-dharma. This is because accepting one thing to the exclusion of all others is termed a demonic activity. Furthermore:
Furthermore, one should know this: since all Buddha-dharmas emerge from this sutra, then all dharmas are themselves this sutra.
It is like gold fashioned into various vessels; thus, all those various vessels are gold.

Therefore, one knows that among the six perfections and the myriad practices, there is nothing that is not *prajñā*. If one were to falsely reckon that this *prajñā* is a separate dharma existing independently—
That which excels other dharmas would then become a non-dharma. As for the phrase "even as little as a four-line verse," this clarifies that it refers to the absolute minimum;
even if a small portion of the text encompasses the full meaning, it is fit to be called a single verse, without being restricted to a specific reference.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have the thought, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A stream-enterer is called one who has entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore he is called a stream-enterer. Subhūti, at that time...
"What do you think? Does a Sakṛdāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? The name 'Sakṛdāgāmin' means 'one who comes back once,' yet in reality there is no coming or going."
This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought:
‘I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin’? Subhūti replied: “No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
An Anāgāmin is called ‘one who does not return,’ yet in reality there is no such thing as non-returning; therefore he is called an Anāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think?
"How is it? Can an Arhat have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma named 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span."
"World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention and am foremost among men;
I am a foremost Arhat who is free from desire. World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as 'I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti delights in solitude."
The practitioner of *araṇā* (non-conflict) is Subhūti; because he truly has no practice, he is named Subhūti, who delights in the practice of *araṇā*.
Because there is no differentiation in unconditioned dharmas, the wisdom and abandonment of the four fruits are all non-arising.
"Free from strife, detached from desire, and supremely tranquil; because there is no activity, one thus practices. The commentary states:
This explains the aforementioned doubt regarding how all noble ones (ārya) are differentiated by means of unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
The doubt asks: "If they are called 'unconditioned,' how can there be differentiation? Since there is differentiation, what is [the cause]?"

Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Here it is clarified that the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] equally realize the unconditioned, yet this does not preclude their distinctions. Although there are distinctions, all of them realize the unconditioned;

therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of a srotāpanna, these are the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
up to the wisdom or the abandonment of an arhat, these are the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas."
*Srotāpanna* is translated here as "Entering the Stream" (*yuliu*). It is also translated as "Flowing Against the Stream. To say "entering the stream":

"entering" (*ru*) is equivalent to "entering upon" (*yu*). This is spoken in reference to the flow of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). Alternatively, it is called "flowing against" (*ni*), which is spoken in reference to the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

In reality, there is neither entering nor exiting, neither flowing against nor following. It is only because one turns one's back on awakening and conforms to the defilements that one conventionally designates this as "exiting from the dharma-nature."
Entering into birth and death while turning one’s back on the defilements and uniting with awakening is merely a provisional name for "reversing birth and death" and "anticipating the dharma-nature.
There is nothing that enters, because the unconditioned dharma-nature is devoid of subject and object, and is not among the six sense objects.

Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been deluded by their emotions and false views, failing to escape the realm of the six sense objects, even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are merely subtle mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*) within the sphere of the mind.

When the sixteen moments of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) are perfected and untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) arises, not even the slightest trace of a dharma-characteristic (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) can be perceived. At that time, one first enters the noble stream of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Within the unconditioned, there are still many distinctions; yet those nowadays who rely on obscure realization fail to comprehend these dharma-characteristics and constantly grasp at emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

To take quiescence as the ultimate is to have subject and object remain distinct; yet to hastily claim there is neither subject nor object is much like the mythical tortoise dragging its tail—it sweeps away more than it clears.
One fails to realize that the emptiness of what is grasped does not transcend two types:
first, when the effort of pressing and squeezing reaches its limit, it suddenly causes the world, body, and mind to subside and vanish, like sparks struck from stone or a flash of lightning.
First, like a flash of lightning, one suddenly glimpses emptiness and stillness; this is called "vast and open emptiness" (*hōtatsu-kū*).

Second, having habitually heard the teachings on true emptiness during ordinary times but not yet understanding their essential meaning, when practicing seated meditation, one abandons the state of birth and seeks the state of extinction, aspiring in every thought-moment for the superior realm of emptiness and stillness.
Because of the depth of this practice, the realm of emptiness manifests before one; this is called "emptiness of transformed appearance" (*henzō-kū*). This...

The two kinds of emptiness are both subsumed under the category of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). They are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within meditative concentration.
These are forever not the domain of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized by a *srotāpanna*, because the seeds of their conceptual grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) have not been severed at all.
It is like mistaking a donkey’s saddle-bridge for one’s father’s chin; how could this not be so?
How erroneous! Therefore, in the degenerate age, many wild Chan practitioners often break both precepts and views after attaining these two kinds of emptiness;
thus they bring ruin upon themselves and others. If one were truly a *srotāpanna*, how could they break the precepts? Once the precepts are broken, one is no longer a *srotāpanna*.
How then can such a person arrogantly claim to be an ultimate saint, asserting that there are neither transgressions nor karmic retributions? This applies even to a *sakṛdāgāmin*.

This is called "One Who Returns Once" (*ekābhinivartika*). It refers to one for whom the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm have been exhausted as to the first six grades, while three grades remain;
thus, they go once to the heavens and return once to the human world before attaining the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). To say that there is truly no going and coming means:
It is like holding space within a flask; fundamentally, there is no coming or going. Anāgāmin is called "Non-returner" because their desire and thought have been exhausted;
they enter parinirvāṇa in the higher realms and do not return again to be born in this realm of desire.
It is said that there is truly no one who does not come; yet that realm does not increase, nor does the desire realm decrease. It is like empty space contained within a jar:

when the jar is moved, the empty space of its original location is neither diminished nor increased. Arhats are called "the Unattached," "the Worthy of Offerings," "the Slayers of the Foe," and "the Non-arisen.
This is because they have eternally severed and exhausted all afflictions of the three realms; in truth, there is none [who does not come].

There is a dharma called "non-arising. If there were a non-arising dharma that could be apprehended, then subject and object would be distinct and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) would remain fully present.
Therefore, the Venerable One again recounted his own practice as proof: "Where there is desire, there is contention;
where there is contention, there is clamor and confusion, not true tranquility. If there is apprehension or activity, then there is desire and..."
Regarding "contention": how can it be called "non-contention" and "freedom from desire"? Therefore, the *Acintya-sūtra* says:
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī, "Have you attained the inconceivable? Mañjuśrī replied, "No, World-Honored One. I am myself the inconceivable."
How is it that through the inconceivable one attains the inconceivable? Thus we know that although the great and the small differ, their hidden convergence is one;

therefore, one may cite the four fruits of arhatship to testify to Prajñā. In the dhyāna and lecture traditions of the末代 (final age), each takes what they have attained with a mind of grasping as being correct and others as being wrong, engaging in fervent contention.
Their deviation from the two kinds of emptiness is extreme indeed.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma?
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained no dharma at all."
Awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*);
because there is no arising, no intrinsic nature, and nothing to be attained, it is only when one realizes this state of non-attainment that one is worthy of the prediction of unsurpassed *bodhi*.

The commentary states: Since even the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] cannot be attained, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) likewise cannot be attained. How then can it be said...?

To resolve the doubt as to whether the Buddha attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, it is said that in reality he obtained nothing at all regarding the dharmas.
This "reality of obtaining nothing" is precisely what is called the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
Were there even the slightest dharma to be obtained, it would all be deceptive and false—just like the head of Yan-ruo or the pearl within one's clothing. It is certain.
It is not obtained from another; yet one cannot say that there is no head or no jewel.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called adorning buddha-fields is itself not adorning; it is merely named 'adorning.'
The four kinds of Buddha-fields are all but mind; when the mind is pure, the land is pure, free from contrived effort.
When the deluded mind adorns the land, it is not truly adorned. Knowing that the land is but mind, one attains mastery over adornment.

The Treatise says: Since the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is without anything to be attained, the grasping of Buddha-fields and the teaching of sentient beings are likewise [without attainment].
Furthermore, is there nothing to be attained? To sever this doubt, it is said: "That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not adornment;
it is called adornment. Now, there are four kinds of lands: first, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, which is the place of self-enjoyment;
second, the Land of True Reward; third, the Land of Expedient Means; and fourth, the Land of Shared Dwelling, which is the place for transforming sentient beings. And...
All are not apart from one's own mind. If the ignorance of one's own mind is ultimately and eternally exhausted, then the Land of Constant Quiescent Light is adorned and becomes absolutely pure.
If, for the sake of gathering and transforming the bodhisattva beings within one's own mind, one adorns the Land of True Reward to bring it to purity;
and if, for the sake of gathering and transforming the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha beings within one's own mind, one [adorns...]

One adorns the land of skillful means to bring it to purity. If it is for the sake of gathering and transforming the six classes of ordinary beings within one's own mind, one adorns the land of cohabitation to bring it to purity.
Since the sentient beings to be transformed are not external to one's nature, how could the Buddha-land that is taken up be separate from one's own mind?
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "According as the mind is pure, so the Buddha-land is pure. This is indeed true.
Apart from the nature of the mind, there are no external environments or retributive objects that can be adorned as separate entities.

Therefore, the various sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas arise, according to the power of their cultivation and based upon the karma of the pure mind, within the Buddha-lands existing within the minds of those sentient beings.
That is to say, when the hindrances of the five turbidities are lightened, one is born into the Pure Land of Shared Residence; this is the realization of the Dharma-body.

The severance of delusions gives rise to the purity of expedient means; the perfect and wondrous threefold contemplation gives rise to the purity of retributive fruition; ultimate wisdom and severance give rise to the purity of the serene light.
Since such subjects who transform and those who are transformed, as well as that which gives rise and that which is given rise to, are all solely mind, their nature is free from fabrication.
If one realizes that there is no land outside of mind, the pure mind itself is the pure land; thus, it is adorned throughout the day.
There is no mark of adornment to be grasped, nor is there any dharma of adornment to which one may cling; this is called the true adornment of the Buddha-land.
Within the single nature of mind, one can establish four kinds of lands—pure, impure, and so forth—manifesting them horizontally and vertically with various forms of mastery.
If one does not realize that all is but mind, one falsely claims that there are lands existing outside the mind. Can [this be so]?
Adornments are characterized by marks and are conditioned; since sensory objects are not permanent, it is said that they are "not adornments.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way; they should not...

One should not dwell on form when generating the mind; one should not dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when generating the mind. One should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere.
To generate the mind without dwelling—these two are neither two nor one; realizing this meaning of non-duality is called the pure mind.
The pure mind and the six perfections are the causes for purifying the Buddha-land; therefore, Bodhisattvas should practice and study them.

The Treatise states: This follows upon the aforementioned land adorned with the transcendence of signs (*animitta*), and now correctly demonstrates the practice adorned with the transcendence of signs.
"One should thus give rise to a pure mind" refers precisely to the wondrous practices of the three kinds of giving (*dāna*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

The mind is called "pure" because it does not dwell upon the six sense objects, such as form and so forth. This merely admonishes one not to dwell [upon the six perfections]; it does not teach that one should not give rise to the mind.
Throughout the day the mind arises; throughout the day there is no dwelling. Throughout the day there is no dwelling; throughout the day the mind arises.
It is precisely because the mind arises that there is no dwelling; it is precisely because there is no dwelling that the mind arises. Although this is how it is explained...
There are two [aspects], yet in reality they are not two. Only by realizing this can one be called "pure-minded," and will surely attain the wondrous fruit of the Pure Land.

Thus, when the Sixth Patriarch heard these words, he attained sudden enlightenment into the True Vehicle (*tathāgatayāna*). In later generations, people have clung to the words and become stuck in the phrases, rarely reaching the profound school.
Only Master Youxi’s *Prajñā-rongxin-lun* (Treatise on the Fusion of Mind through Prajñā) offers a glimpse into its inner sanctum; I shall now briefly describe it.

The meaning is as follows: "Non-abiding" means not dwelling in any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). "Generating the mind" means generating the mind for the six perfections and myriad practices.
There are those who generate the mind yet cannot abide in non-abiding; these are the Bodhisattvas of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* (the "event-perfection" Bodhisattvas).
There are those who abide in non-abiding yet cannot generate the mind; these are the followers of the two vehicles of the *Hīnayāna* (the *Śrāvaka* and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles). From... [self...]
There are those who first possess the mind [of awakening] and subsequently attain non-abiding; this refers to the fruits of Buddhahood in the *Nidāna* (Cang) and *Vaipulya* (Tong) teachings.

There are those who first attain non-abiding and subsequently give rise to the mind [of awakening]; this refers to Bodhisattvas who have emerged into the provisional realm (*chujia*). There are also those for whom non-abiding is not the giving rise to the mind.
"Generating the mind is not without abiding" refers to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

"Abiding in non-abiding while generating the mind, and generating the mind while abiding in non-abiding" refers to the stages from the grounds upward in the Distinct Teaching, as well as from the stage of the Name (*mingziwei*) onward in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Although the Distinct Teaching pertains to dharmas outside the [three] realms, regarding these two meanings, it initially still distinguishes between them, though later they become unified.
Second: Only those who practice the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) understand from beginning to end that [reality] is non-dual.
Therefore, perfect contemplation is the true cause for the Pure Land. Furthermore, all ordinary beings falsely grasp at and cling to the various phenomena within the triple world.

One constantly dwells amidst the six sense objects; yet when investigated to the ultimate degree, mind and objects shift and change in succession—when has there ever been any dwelling? This is called "in principle, non-dwelling.

All followers of the Two Vehicles delude themselves regarding the partial truth, extinguishing their minds and suppressing their wisdom, thereby departing from the birth-and-death of the segmented realm.

To speak exhaustively according to principle: transformation and change remain entirely present; how could it ever not be arising? This is called "the mind arising as the very essence of principle" (*li-ji-sheng-xin*).
The person of perfect enlightenment understands that abiding is non-abiding, and non-arising is arising.

From this comes the name "the mind arising as non-abiding" (*wu-zhu-sheng-xin*), continuing up to the ultimate "the mind arising as non-abiding. Furthermore, that which is called "non-abiding" does not abide in arising.
Death. Not abiding in nirvana; not abiding in the two extremes; not abiding in the middle way—therefore it is called "non-abiding.

As for the phrase "generating the mind," it means generating the mind that seeks the supreme [enlightenment], generating the mind that transforms those below, generating the mind that subdues, and generating the mind that gathers and sustains.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm and exhausting the three periods of time—therefore it is called "generating the mind. Nowadays, when people hear of emptiness, they immediately grasp at emptiness.
This is not even the meaning of a small portion of non-abiding, let alone the arising of a pure mind.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body were like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be large? Subhūti said:
"It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that it is 'not a body'; it is called 'large' only by name."
The body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which excels all; yet it does not grasp at the thought, "I am this mountain king.
The retribution-body of the Buddha is likewise not a [substantial] body; because it is free from discrimination, it is called the "Great Body."
The treatise says: If one does not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*), how can the Buddhas attain the all-pervading body of mastery?
To sever this doubt, it is said that "that which is not a body is called the Great Body. An ancient commentary states:
"Just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is called 'great' because its power is lofty and far-reaching, yet it does not grasp at the substance of that mountain-king."
I am the King of Mountains. Because I am free from conceptual discrimination, I receive the retribution of bliss; the Buddha is also like this.
Because he has attained the essence of the Unsurpassed Dharma King, he is called "Great Body," yet he does not grasp at that essence of the Dharma King, thinking, "I am the Dharma King.
This is because he is free from conceptual discrimination. Furthermore, Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is but a partial metaphor, for that—
It is the Mountain King because it is not any other mountain. The Buddha takes the dharma-realm as his body; it is not like the Mountain King being called "great" in contrast to small things.
All dharmas are identical to the Buddha’s body; this is called the "Great Body."
"Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied, "They would be very numerous, World-Honored One.
Those Ganges Rivers alone would already be immeasurably many, let alone their sands. Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if...
"Suppose there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and used them for giving.
Would they gain much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a good son or a good daughter, from within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold four..."
To explain such verses and so forth to others, the merit of this [act] surpasses the former merit.
Guṇadatta said: "Why was this superior analogy not presented first?

It is because ordinary people, having not yet seen the truth, would not give rise to faith and understanding if it were explained extensively at the outset; rather, they develop faith by hearing it gradually. Furthermore:
The merit of upholding [this teaching] is vast. It achieves such merit through thirteen kinds of causes, namely:

because it is situated in a state worthy of reverence; because it is honored by noble persons; because it is the supreme cause for all excellence; because its meaning is unsurpassed; because it transcends both internal and external profusion; because it is the cause for the superior physical form of a Buddha;
because it surpasses the merit of internal giving; because it is coextensive with the appearance of a Buddha; and because it is rare and difficult to encounter.
Because of faith and understanding; because of the difficulty of practicing; because of the greatness of the fruit of faithful cultivation; because of the accomplishment of faith and understanding;
and because of unsurpassed power. For what reason, World-Honored One, do you so earnestly explain these various causes and characteristics?
