It is because sentient beings practice the giving of material sustenance and seek the fruits of wealth and status, rather than upholding the True Dharma to sever the causes of all suffering.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—
including its devas, humans, and asuras— as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
The Treatise says: This place itself is worthy of veneration, for it is the site where the Wheel of Dharma was turned.
How much more so for a person who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it!
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and foremost rare and marvelous Dharma. Wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha. If...

"Honoring the Disciples. The Commentary states: This refers to those who are worthy of veneration. To receive [the teaching] without contradiction is called "receiving" (śruta); to never forget it from beginning to end is called "retaining" (dhāraṇa);

to read from the scroll is called "reading" (vācana); and to recite from memory when separated from the scroll is called "reciting" (svādhyāya). The most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma is precisely Bodhi...
"Tiye. Because it is accomplished, it is worthy of veneration. That which is not the fruit is the fruit; therein lies the Buddha. That which is not the cause is the cause;
therein lie the venerable disciples, such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. [The text says: "How much more so for those who...
Such persons are worthy of veneration. "Wherever the sūtras reside... This Dharma is worthy of being esteemed. By means of the written words...
Because it abides in the world and is able to transmit the Dharma of the true nature of cause and effect, it may also be divided into two kinds of causes for merit.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it? The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By this name..."
"Memorize this, Subhūti; you should uphold it. Why is that? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not a *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is merely designated as the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Treatise says: This is the supreme cause of all things. To practice it in accordance with it is "reverence"; to propagate it extensively is "upholding.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* destroys delusion; there is no delusion that is not exhausted. It illuminates principle; there is no principle that is not revealed.

Yet its essence is neither destruction nor revelation, for *prajñā* is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and is identical with all phenomena (*dharma*). There is no separate phenomenon that is named *prajñā*.
Therefore, because all dharmas are *prajñā*, one should uphold them in this way.
Being able to ultimately reach the fundamental source and the ultimate limit of both mundane and supramundane phenomena is called a *pāramitā*.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has preached nothing."
The Treatise says: This is precisely that meaning which is unsurpassed. Because within the Prajñāpāramitā the nature of words is detached, it cannot be explained or grasped by means of words;
therefore, it is said that "in forty-nine years not a single word was spoken.
This refers to speaking all day long without speaking, rather than regarding silence as non-speaking. If it were not...
Having realized the supreme meaning, he remained silent;
for even that silence is a mental verbalization. Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms in a trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has spoken of are not atoms.
"Dust. This is called "minute dust. The Tathāgata says that the world is not a world; this is called the world. The Commentary states:
This refers to transcending both the internal and the external many. "Minute dust" refers to the environment (the *niśraya-vipāka*); "world" refers to sentient beings.
Since minute dust is not minute dust, then minute dust is not many, yet the merit of upholding the sutra is great; thus it is said to "transcend."
Externally, there is much. If the world were not a world, then sentient beings would not be many; yet the merit of upholding this sutra is great, surpassing even that internal abundance.
Furthermore, the ignorant and foolish do not understand that all phenomena are mind-only; they claim that the world is formed by the accumulation of atoms.
The world is analyzed into atoms, yet one does not know that atoms are not atoms; how then can they be accumulated to form a world?

A world is not a world; how then can it be analyzed into atoms? Only the Bodhisattva of Prajñā understands that atoms and the world lack any real nature; therefore, it is said that they are "not atoms" and "not a world. Thus he understands.
The nature of non-nature is precisely the true nature of atoms and worlds; therefore, it is said, "this is called atoms and worlds.
This thus clarifies both emptiness and existence simultaneously, wherein negation and illumination are non-dual. For this reason, its merit and virtue are transcendentally supreme.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the thirty-two marks are in fact no-marks; they are merely designated as the "thirty-two marks."
The treatise states: This is precisely the cause for the superior form-body of a Buddha.

If one relies on the thirty-two marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), where one mark is accomplished by accumulating a hundred merits—such as the merit of curing the blindness of all beings in a great trichiliocosm—then the accumulation of merit serves as the cause.

However, if one does not realize that the *dharmakāya* is the fundamental source, nor realize that the marks and signs are inherently complete within the nature, then [one merely understands] the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) and *saṃbhogakāya*.
Marks ultimately revert to impermanence; how can one perceive the Tathāgata through these? A Bodhisattva of Prajñā deeply knows that the Dharmakāya is not a mark, yet it possesses all marks.
Whichever single mark one grasps, each is immediately an ocean of marks as numerous as motes of dust in a buddha-field, inconceivable.
How could one definitively form a conceptual understanding of marks? Therefore it is said: "This is precisely the absence of marks. This is called the subtle and wondrous.
The pure Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks; each and every mark is the Dharma-realm.

Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in acts of charity, [the merit would not equal that of one who hears this teaching].

If, moreover, there should be someone who, from this sutra, even receives and upholds as little as a four-line verse and explains it for others, their merit will be exceedingly great. The commentary says:
This surpasses the merit of internal giving. From the seven treasures up to one’s kingdom, cities, wife, and children—these are called [external giving].

External giving consists of giving material things. Giving one’s own body and life is called internal giving. Although the merit of internal giving is many times greater, it can never equal that of upholding this sutra.

This is because giving one’s body does not necessarily sever the causes for further embodiment, whereas the Dharma-giving of upholding this sutra can sever the causes of birth and death for both oneself and others.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and said to the Buddha:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this.
Since the past, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."
The Treatise says: This is identical to the appearance of a Buddha in the world. When a Buddha arises in the world, those of meager merit find it difficult to encounter him;
this sutra is likewise so, for few have heard it in advance. Subhūti followed the Buddha’s awakening, yet even in the past he had not heard this True Dharma;
therefore, its rarity is equal to the appearance of a Buddha.

“World-Honored One, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and, with pure faith, gives rise to the mark of reality, you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
World-Honored One, this mark of reality is precisely the absence of marks.”
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The Commentary states: This refers to the rare ability to believe and understand. When the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is purified and one ascends to the five grades of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), it is called "attaining hearing.

When the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is purified, defilements fall away and the faculties become pure; this is called "the purity of the mind of faith. It is the accomplishment of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

To analyze and reveal [the nature of phenomena] is called the arising of the true mark (*dharmatā*). To spontaneously and decisively reach the fruit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is called the accomplishment of the foremost rare merit.
Although the true mark is non-arising, it is said to "arise"; this is as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
although all phenomena do not arise, the *prajñā* arises. This is because understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising is itself [the arising of *prajñā*].
The wisdom that contemplates non-arising manifests; this is what is called "arising. That which is the true mark is precisely the absence of marks:
it is not a mark of existence, not a mark of non-existence, not a mark of both existence and non-existence, and not a mark of neither existence nor non-existence.
To state it briefly: it is free from all marks, yet it is all dharmas. Being free is itself the negation of freedom; being thus is itself the negation of being thus. Therefore—
“World-Honored One,
it would not be difficult for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it. However,
if in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it— such persons [would be even more rare].”
This is indeed the foremost rarity.

The Treatise says: This refers to the practice that is difficult to achieve. In the final age, when obstacles are profound, to have faith, understanding, and to receive and uphold [this teaching] is all the more rare.
Why is this? This person has no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of beings, and no mark of a life-span.
Why is that? The mark of self is precisely no-mark; the marks of others, beings, and a life-span are likewise no-marks.
Why is this? To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas.

The Commentary states: This refers to the greatness of the fruit of faith and cultivation. Even if one were to conceive even the slightest notion of a self, a person, or other such characteristics, one could never believe in this sutra.

Conversely, if one believes in, understands, and upholds this sutra, one will certainly be able to penetrate the fact that the characteristics of a self, a person, and so forth, are in their very essence signless (*animitta*).
It is like when cataracts are cleared away and the floating hairs vanish; the very place where the flowers appeared is emptiness.

This is not a matter of destroying the flowers to grasp at emptiness. Therefore, to be free from all marks of flowers and likewise free from the separate grasping of the mark of emptiness is what is called the Buddhas’ realization of the great fruit.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is exceedingly rare."
The Commentary states: "This refers to the accomplishment of faith and understanding. The Sub-commentary says: "To be momentarily startled is called 'alarm' (*jing*);

for the heart and gallbladder to be timid and weak is called 'fear' (*bu*); to deeply loathe a prior matter is called 'dread' (*wei*). Furthermore, alarm pertains to the beginner; fear pertains to the Two Vehicles."

They fear these non-Buddhists. Furthermore, upon first hearing the sutra they are not startled; next, when reflecting upon it, they are not terrified; and finally, when practicing it, they do not feel fear.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the "foremost pāramitā" is, in fact, not the foremost pāramitā.
Honey. This is called the first *pāramitā*.
The Commentary says: This is indeed the unsurpassed sovereign power (*anuttara-prabhāva*). According to the *Guṇadatta-śāstra*, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the first *pāramitā*—Subhūti, this first *pāramitā* is [as follows]..."
To explain: those immeasurable Buddhas also speak in this same way. The commentary asks: why is it called "foremost"?
Because there is nothing equal to it. Why is there nothing equal to it? Because its power is supreme among all the Buddha-dharmas.
Because all Buddhas preach in concert. Yet, this sutra contains no passage stating that all Buddhas preach it together;
it simply says, "It is not the foremost *pāramitā*; it is called the foremost *pāramitā*. One should know that the foremost *pāramitā* encompasses all dharmas;
there is not a single dharma that is exclusively the foremost, nor is there a single dharma that...
This is not the foremost. Just as all that is governed by a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) constitutes the realm of that king, if there were no Wheel-Turning King, there would be nothing governed;
and if there were nothing governed, one could not be called a Wheel-Turning King.
This concludes the explanation of the thirteen kinds of causes. The merit of upholding this sutra exceeds that of bestowing precious gifts. To summarize this in verse:
Dwelling in honor and esteemed by men, his sutras are equal to the Buddha’s;
All supreme causes, their meaning unsurpassed, transcending the many superior causes of both internal and external forms. Surpassing internal meritorious giving, he manifests like the Buddha;
rare indeed is the ability to believe and understand, difficult is the practice to perform. The fruit is great and accomplished, its majesty unsurpassed.
Therefore, Subhūti, the merit of one who receives, maintains, and explains this sutra is incomparable to the merit of giving away as many jewels as there are sands in the Ganges River.
Regarding the perfection of patience, the Tathāgata says it is not the perfection of patience; it is called the perfection of patience.
Why is this? Subhūti, as when in the past my body was cut to pieces by King Kali...
Subhūti, at that time, I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why was this?

If, when my limbs were severed joint by joint in the past, I had possessed a perception of a self, a perception of a person, a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.
Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I practiced patience.
"O Venerable One, throughout all those worlds, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should set their mind on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining detached from all marks.
They should not give rise to the mind by dwelling upon forms; they should not give rise to the mind by dwelling upon sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas."
One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not dwelling at all. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form when practicing giving. Subhūti, this is because a bodhisattva acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.
"One should give in this manner. Thus has the Tathāgata spoken: 'All marks are, in fact, no-marks. Furthermore, he has said:
'All sentient beings are, in fact, no-sentient-beings.'"
Patience is itself Prajñā, free from the four marks; the three kinds of giving and the six perfections are likewise so.
Therefore, one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere, benefiting all beings who are like illusions.
The Treatise says: If within the Buddha-dharma only Prajñā is supreme, why must one further cultivate other practices? [This is] for the purpose of dispelling...
Because of this doubt, it is said that "patience is itself not patience," and so forth.
This is because all practices are subsumed by *prajñā*, for all practices are themselves *prajñā*. Consequently, past sublime practices are cited as evidence.

Regarding the statement "the mark of selflessness (*anātman-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth," this refers directly to the thorough realization of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), such that one does not give rise to notions of self, person, and so on; yet it is not a state of mere insentient dullness.
To be without perception—were one to be as dull and devoid of discrimination as this—it would constitute ignorance. With ignorance as the cause, thoughts of aversion arise once more.
Even if one were ultimately like wood or stone, it would still not be the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*. Now, therefore, one observes with right wisdom.

Having realized that the self and persons are fundamentally empty, he gave rise to great compassion for the wicked king and made a great vow to be the very first to deliver him upon his attainment of Buddhahood.
It should be known that for five hundred lifetimes he served as the Rishi of Forbearance, practicing the Prajñāpāramitā for a long time.
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should likewise give rise to the mind of awakening while remaining detached from signs.
Regarding the mind, "being free from signs" means not dwelling upon the signs of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
"Generating the mind" means constantly giving rise to the great bodhicitta. If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not dwelling as it ought to dwell.

Having realized non-dwelling, one should practice the sublime conduct of the three kinds of giving (*tri-dāna*). One must certainly not, on account of practicing giving, subsequently become attached to the six [sense-objects].
Furthermore, one must not harbor expectations that the mind will remain unattached and consequently cease the three kinds of giving;

this is because the Dharma of a Bodhisattva is intended to benefit all sentient beings. Moreover, fearing that people might give rise to the view of emptiness—wondering how one can practice giving to benefit beings if it is said that one must be free from all marks—he explains: "The Tathāgata speaks of one..."
All marks, when realized in their essence, are themselves non-marks; it is not that one negates marks and seeks non-marks elsewhere.
Furthermore, fearing that people might give rise to the view of existence, one asks: "Since it is said to benefit sentient beings, how can there be no mark of sentient beings?"
Therefore, it is explained: "Furthermore, it is said that all sentient beings are not sentient beings.

This is precisely intended for people to practice giving that involves both the presence of characteristics and the departure from characteristics, thereby benefiting the illusory assembly of beings who are themselves non-arising.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, speaks without deception, and speaks without contradiction.
Subhūti, as for the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
Without falsehood and without delusion, it must accord with principle; not being deceptive, it can fully illuminate and verify from beginning to end that phenomena are neither real nor unreal.
For these reasons, one should believe this treatise with earnest attention.
The Treatise says: If all Buddhas are free from all conceptualizations and have realized that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, by what characteristics does the world perceive them?
How can this be believed? To sever such doubts, it is said that he speaks words of truth and so forth. "Truth" means being without falsehood.
For example, worldly people, for the sake of fame and profit, claim to have realized what they have not realized; this is false speech. The Tathāgata is not like this.
Because he has directly realized unsurpassed great enlightenment, it is truly real and not false. For example, there are people in the world who are greedy, base, and deceitful;

though they once attained supernatural powers, they know for themselves that they have already lost them. When someone comes to question them, they merely claim they obtained them previously—this is false speech.
The Tathāgata is not like this, for he has no retrogression or loss regarding great enlightenment. "Like" (yathā) means according to principle; it serves as an analogy.
For example, when worldly people cultivate and attain the four dhyānas, their minds temporarily do not arise and are identical to quiescence; they then say to others, "I have realized nirvāṇa.
This name does not accord with reality. The Tathāgata is not like this, for he has truly realized great nirvāṇa.
To be non-deceptive means to be free from illusion and falsehood. For instance, it is like a fool [who mistakes] a city in the sky, a magical illusion, or a reflection in a mirror.

Regarding such things as the moon in water and a mirage, to conceive of them as existent when they are not, and to give rise to false grasping and attachment through various forms of speech, is called deceptive speech.
The Tathāgata is not like this; he has realized the true nature of phenomena (dharmas), for he possesses the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Non-different" means that there is no duality between the beginning and the end. For example, a master of arts may, through his skill, make remote conjectures regarding past and future events;
he might say they are so or not so, or that they ought to be or ought not to be, and thus his words differ [from reality]. The Tathāgata is not like this.
With the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, he universally illumines the three periods of time, penetratingly comprehending the beginning and the end without exception. Observe him...
For a long time, as if it were this very day, until the end of the future limit, he has seen and known all things; for the principles and phenomena he has taught are entirely without difference.
Furthermore, the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas.
This true nature is "no-nature"; the nature of no-nature is what constitutes true nature. Even if one were to grasp at anything among all dharmas...

If one clings [to them], then true speech becomes false speech, because one gives rise to views regarding words and views regarding phenomena, failing to know that their actual nature is fundamentally without nature.

If one does not grasp at or cling to any phenomena, then false speech becomes true speech, because one does not give rise to views regarding words or views regarding phenomena, realizing that the absence of nature is itself the actual nature. Therefore, it is said: "This dharma..."
"It is neither real nor unreal. These five words—such is this sublime Dharma—and it should be believed with true conviction.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.
But if a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling upon dharmas, it is like a person with eyes in the light of the sun.
Illumination, the seeing of various forms,
the arousal of the mind for practice, and wisdom-illumination— these three factors mutually support one another without priority or sequence,
like the sun, visible forms, and light; they successively assist one another to fulfill the function of vision.
The treatise says: If dharmas are without arising and without intrinsic nature, being neither real nor false, they are precisely the ultimate body (*paramārtha-kāya*) of all Buddhas.
For what reason must Bodhisattvas practice giving and so forth? Since they have already practiced giving with such fervor, why is it further said that they do not dwell in dharmas?
To dispel this doubt, the two metaphors of light and darkness are explained: to grasp at signs is darkness; to penetrate [reality] is...
The principle is clear. Here, the eye is used as a metaphor for the mind that has been awakened; the various colors represent the ten thousand practices of the three kinds of giving;
and the sunlight represents the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*. Inferring from the meaning of this metaphor:

if one does not awaken the mind, then even while constantly dwelling within the luminous realm of *prajñā* and the ten thousand practices, one will see nothing at all—just as when the sunlight shines brightly [but one is blind].

Although there are various forms, one who lacks eyes will ultimately see nothing. Likewise, if the myriad practices are absent, then the arousal of the bodhicitta and prajñā would be rendered in vain.
It is like having various colors but no eyes or sun—what use would they be?
These two metaphors are now cited specifically for the sake of explaining the Bodhisattva who practices giving. Therefore, only these two examples are provided.

Subhūti, in a future age, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows these persons and fully sees these persons;
they shall all achieve immeasurable and boundless merit. Subhūti, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family...

During the first part of the day, he gives away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; during the middle part of the day, he again gives away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and during the final part of the day, he likewise gives away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

In this manner, he gives his body in sacrifice for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas. Yet, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and, with a faithful heart, does not oppose it—
The merit of that person would be superior to theirs; how much more so for one who writes it down, receives and maintains it, reads and recites it, and explains it to others.
Subhūti, to speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle. If there is anyone who can receive, maintain, and read it...
Recite it and explain it extensively for others. The Tathāgata fully knows these people; the Tathāgata fully sees these people.
They all attain and accomplish immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Such people as these, Subhūti, are indeed carrying upon their shoulders the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata. Why is this? Subhūti, if...

Those who delight in inferior dharmas—namely, those ordinary worldlings and outsiders who are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span—will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be, it should be honored by all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras; you should know that such a place is [a sacred site].
This is precisely that stūpa; all should pay homage with reverence, circumambulate it, and scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family who upholds, recites, and studies this sūtra is treated with contempt by others, their past-life karmic offenses—which would otherwise have caused them to fall into the evil realms—are [exhausted] because they are now being treated with contempt by people in this world. Their previous...
The worldly karmic offenses will be immediately extinguished, and one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty million *nayuta* of Buddhas;
I made offerings to and served them all, none of whom were passed by in vain. If...

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there are good men or good women who, in the future final age, are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain will not be matched by even a hundredth part of the merit from my own offerings to the Buddhas;
nor by a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor even by any calculation, number, or analogy can it be reached.
Subhūti, if good men or good women, in the future final age...

If I were to fully describe the merit obtained by those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, some people, upon hearing it, would have their minds become deranged and would harbor doubts and fail to believe.
Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable.
The karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
To receive, uphold, read, and recite this is itself the Tathāgata.
The accomplishment of merit and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—great matters and great times—cannot equal it; for this is the Mahāyāna, the Supreme Vehicle.
To shoulder the burden of Bodhi, even the small are unable; wherever it passes, it is a stupa and should be honored.
It extinguishes past karma and brings realization of Bodhi, eternally surpassing the merits of Buddhas of the past.
To explain this fully would cause those of shallow understanding to doubt, for its meaning and its karmic retribution are inconceivable.

The Commentary states: This extensively elucidates the meritorious fruits and retributions of upholding [this teaching]. First, it provides a general indication, stating: "To uphold, recite, and chant it is to be the Tathāgata.
This is because one has profoundly realized the true nature (dharmatā) and understands that all sentient beings are no different from the Buddha;
from the initial stage of mere names to the ultimate stage, every position is itself the Buddha. Next, it says: "By..."

The Buddha’s wisdom fully knows and fully sees all things, such as knowing and seeing how results are achieved from causes, and [the continuity of] this life and future lives—all such meritorious qualities.
Next, his merits are revealed through eight kinds of excellence. First:
It cannot be equaled by great deeds or long periods of time. A body as vast as the sands of the Ganges is called a "great deed.
An incalculable number of eons is called a "long period of time. Even with such giving, it still does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra.
While Bodhisattvas possessing the five supernormal powers can also perform such acts of giving through these means, they do not compare to this sutra, which directly severs the outflow of ignorance.
For these reasons, secondly, this sutra was taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set their minds upon the Great Vehicle and the Supreme Vehicle;

it is not common to the three vehicles. The teaching of Prajñāpāramitā is called the Great Vehicle, and within the Great Vehicle, it is intended solely for the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching].
They are called those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.

Third, such persons as these are indeed carrying the burden of unsurpassed bodhi, because they receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching], and extensively explain it for others, thereby perpetuating the lineage of the Buddhas so that it shall not be severed.
Fourth, it sustains and operates like one carrying a heavy burden.

Fifth, those who delight in the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle cannot even receive its teaching, let alone ordinary people attached to a self or non-Buddhists attached to [wrong] views; thus, none of them are capable of bearing it. Fifth, wherever this sutra exists...
This is precisely because the *dharmakāya* and the *śarīra* relics are fully present within this stūpa.
Sixth, it extinguishes past karma, transforming what is heavy into light so that one no longer falls into the evil realms. Seventh, one shall attain *bodhi*, for once karma has been extinguished.
Because the essence of bodhi is inherently luminous and pure. Eighth, it surpasses the merit of the Tathāgata’s past encounters with Buddhas.
Although the Tathāgata encountered many Buddhas in the past prior to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he still maintained a mind that grasps at attainment and had not yet realized the signless;
thus, he did not receive a prediction of enlightenment. Therefore, this does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra. This is seen in the [Sutra].
Dīpaṃkara Buddha attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that time, he was for the first time in constant accord with Prajñā.
Because it possesses these eight kinds of excellence, those of shallow understanding will certainly be unable to believe it when it is explained in full detail;
therefore, it is summarized by saying that its meaning is inconceivable and its retribution is likewise inconceivable.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
One should give rise to this thought: "I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa;
yet, once all sentient beings have been brought to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva. And why is that? Subhūti...
In enlightenment, there is truly no dharma that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There is neither one who gives rise to the mind, nor one who abides, nor one who subdues; yet the mind should abide and be subdued.
Furthermore, there is not a single dharma existing apart from the mind. Thus, the pure cause is fully revealed.

The Commentary states: This section further eliminates the subtle grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) within the minds of Bodhisattvas, so that they may be completely purified without remainder.
Since the preceding passage has already clearly elucidated the true meaning of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), how could there be anything remaining unexhausted?
There are briefly two reasons for this further inquiry: first, since the meaning is such as it is—inconceivable—how could one possibly find a place to settle therein? Thus, all... [text continues]
When a bodhisattva resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), how ultimately should they abide? How should they subdue their mind?

Second, having said that one "resolves upon the mind," one then thinks, "I am able to resolve upon the mind. Having said that one "abides in non-abiding," one then thinks, "I am able to abide without abiding.
Having said that one "subdues the mind," one then thinks, "I am able to subdue the mind. Thus, the notion of a self and dharmas remains manifest.
However, how can one attain correspondence with Prajñā? This is specifically for those of dull faculties who seek further expedient means;
the Buddha again declares: "One who has resolved upon Bodhicitta should give rise to such a mind," and so on, up to "it is not a Bodhisattva," etc.
This was to answer his request regarding how, in the ultimate sense, one should abide and subdue the mind. Next, he again answers:

It is said: "In truth, there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta. This means to sweep away the egoistic attachment to the notion that "I can give rise to the mind," as well as the attachments to non-abiding and subduing.
For the one who gives rise to the mind does so simply by taking the entirety of the nature (xing) as cultivation (xiu), and keeping the entirety of cultivation within the nature.
The characteristics of the mind itself cannot be apprehended; how then could there be a separate dharma that causes the mind to arise?
Since the mind lacks the characteristics of a mind, where can the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha) exist? Since unreal dharmas do not arise, where can the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) exist?

When the afflictions of the emotions are thus purified, Prajñā manifests before one. Being neither falsely existent, nor merely empty, it transcends words and is beyond all predication; through this, it is fundamentally pure.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma called ‘anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’?

“No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there was no dharma that the Buddha obtained as ‘anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’ while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. The Buddha said, “So it is...”
"So it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.'"
Śākyamuni. In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me the prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni. Why is this?
Because "Tathāgata" is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas. If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata...
[He] attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, in truth there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are...
"This is the Buddha-dharma. Subhūti, that which is called 'all dharmas' is itself not all dharmas; therefore it is called 'all dharmas.
Subhūti, it is like a person whose body is tall and large. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, what the Tathāgata calls a 'tall and large body' is itself not a large body; it is called a 'large body.'"
Because there is nothing to be attained, the fruit is likewise so; No dharma can be apprehended, yet one receives the prediction [of enlightenment].
All dharmas are non-dharmas; this is called the Buddha-dharma. The Great Body is no body; this is called the Buddha-body. The Treatise says:
If it is said that in reality there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta, how can there be the conferring of a prediction? How could there be such a thing?

The Buddha [taught] the matter of attaining the fruit of bodhi. To dispel this doubt, he clarified that since not even a single dharma can be obtained as a cause, not even a single dharma can be obtained as a fruit.
Only when there is nothing at all to be obtained is one fit for the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
If there were even the slightest dharma to be obtained, it would not correspond to the true nature (*tathatā*) of all dharmas; how then could one be granted the prediction of becoming a Buddha?
"Buddha" means "Tathāgata. Regarding the meaning of "all phenomena are suchness" (tathatā): all phenomena are fundamentally true suchness;
their nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, neither changing nor differing. Now, not departing from the self-nature of phenomena, he has come to achieve perfect enlightenment;
therefore, he is named Tathāgata. If one says that the Tathāgata attains and realizes bodhi, this is conventional discourse and not the ultimate truth.
The enlightenment attained by the Tathāgata is precisely the self-nature of the mind itself; since there is nothing external that can be added to it, it is not real.
Because one has truly attained non-erroneous awakening and awakened to the self-nature of all phenomena, it is not false.
Furthermore, because enlightenment is not any phenomenon, it is not real; because all phenomena are themselves enlightenment, it is not false.
Furthermore, all dharmas are themselves bodhi; therefore, bodhi has no reality. Bodhi is not distinct from all dharmas;
therefore, bodhi has no falsity. That all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma is because there is nothing outside the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Because the dharma-realm is unchanging yet constantly follows conditions, it is called "all dharmas. Because the dharma-realm follows conditions yet is constantly unchanging, it is "not all dharmas.
Every single dharma is thus unchanging while following conditions, and following conditions while remaining unchanging.
Because it is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, it is called "all dharmas. Realizing this *dharmadhātu* is termed the *dharmakāya*.
The *dharmakāya* is free from all marks and is identical to all dharmas; there is no separate body apart from them, and thus it is not a "great body" in the conventional sense.
Because the *dharmadhātu* constitutes its body, it is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*). This is the sublime adornment of perfect enlightenment that returns to non-attainment.
It is a rigid attachment, Subhūti.
It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they should say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," they cannot be called a bodhisattva.
Why is that? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that is named "bodhisattva. This is...
Therefore, the Buddha has taught that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the adornment of the buddha-fields is itself not an adornment; it is merely designated as an adornment. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva...
One who thoroughly penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena is called by the Tathāgata a true Bodhisattva.
Since neither the one who crosses over nor the one who is crossed over can be apprehended, and the same applies to the adornment and that which is adorned—
thoroughly penetrating the absence of self and the absence of phenomena, one should cultivate this pure, true cause.

The Commentary states: This follows the preceding extensive explanation of the wondrous fruit of non-attainment (*anupalabdhi*), and serves as an exhortation to cultivate the true cause of non-attainment.
Indeed, it is not merely that there are no sentient beings outside the mind to be saved, nor any Buddha-lands outside the mind to be adorned;

even within this very nature of mind (*cittatā*), if one seeks a single substantial dharma (*dravyadharma*) that acts as the savior or the saved, or that which adorns or is adorned, it is utterly unfindable.
It is attained because the nature of subject and object is precisely the self-nature of the mind itself; for there is not even the slightest trace of a self or phenomena that can be apprehended.
To penetrate this in such a manner is what is called being a true Bodhisattva; it does not mean that there is a "one who penetrates."
There is thorough penetration. Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "It is so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye. Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "It is so, World-Honored One; [the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye]."
He possesses the divine eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom eye?
"Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma eye?
"Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha eye?
"No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. Subhūti, what do you think?
Regarding all the sands in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say they are sand? "Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata says they are sand.
"Subhūti, what do you think? If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River..."
"As many as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, so many are the Buddha-worlds. Would they not be very many?
"They would be very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti: "In all those lands, however many kinds of minds there may be among all sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows them all.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all these minds are 'not-minds'; it is for this reason that they are called 'minds'."
Why is that? Subhūti, the past mind is unapprehendable; the present mind is unapprehendable;
the future mind is unapprehendable. Subhūti, what do you think?
If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? "It is so, World-Honored One."
"Venerable One, by this cause and condition, this person gains exceedingly great merit.
Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one gains much merit; because merit is insubstantial, the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit."

Endowed with the five eyes, one attains Bodhi; Clearly seeing realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the mind is no-mind, and merit is no-merit. Therefore, subject and object are eternally quiescent.
The commentary states: The above clarifies the true cause of purity—ultimate non-self and non-dharmas—which constitutes the realm of the Buddha.

There is the doubt that conditioned phenomena do not exist; to dispel this doubt, the Tathāgata’s five eyes are revealed. They are "existent" yet not existent, for the minds and merits of sentient beings are "non-existent" yet not non-existent.
By mutually manifesting existence and non-existence, they skillfully subside conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Now, the five eyes are the cognitive vision that illuminates; the various minds of sentient beings and their merit from giving are the objects illuminated.
If one uses the subsequent to illustrate the prior, then since that which is illuminated already exists, how could the illuminator alone be non-existent?

If one uses the subsequent to illustrate the prior, then since that which is illuminated is already non-existent, how could the illuminator alone be existent? It is simply because the five eyes of the Tathāgata are not understood by ordinary, ignorant people;
because they do not understand them, they falsely reckon them to be non-existent. Therefore, I now specifically clarify their existence to manifest this truth.

It is not an emptiness of annihilation. It is the merit of the minds of the multitude, which the ignorant and foolish grasp at and become attached to. Because of this attachment, they falsely reckon it to be real;
therefore, I now specifically clarify its non-existence to reveal that it lacks an inherent nature. Regarding the "five eyes," they are described in sequential order:
the fleshly eye is the same as that of ordinary humans and sees forms present before one; the divine eye is the same as that of the devas and sees forms beyond obstructions; the wisdom-eye...
The Dharma-eye manifests as being identical to that of the two vehicles, seeing the ultimate truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The Buddha-eye is not shared with the three vehicles; it sees the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If spoken of in terms of perfect interfusion, one eye is all eyes, and all eyes are one eye, universally illuminating the three truths without exception. Therefore, this is also known.
One knows the distinctions among those lands; one also knows the distinctions among the minds of those beings.
One knows that distinction is itself non-distinction. One also knows the extent of their merit, and knows that merit is not real.
If there is neither distinction nor non-distinction, and neither merit nor non-merit, then one should know that the five eyes are themselves not five eyes. If they are one...
Regarding the statement that the obstruction to wondrous wisdom is analytically explained as the five eyes:
one should know that within a single dharma-realm, there are analytically explained various worlds, various mentalities of sentient beings, various causes for giving, and various fruits of merit;
this too is neither erroneous nor mistaken. Based on conventional designations, the illuminator and the illuminated are all clearly manifest; yet based on reality—
Regarding the contemplation of meaning: the object perceived has no separate existence from the subject, and the subject perceiving has no separate existence from the object;
therefore, it is said to be eternally quiescent. Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Buddha be seen by means of a body endowed with physical form? "No, World-Honored One."
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the body of perfect form. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the body of perfect form is itself not a body of perfect form; it is merely designated as the "body of perfect form. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of all the marks? "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of the possession of..."

One should not perceive [the Tathāgata] by means of various marks. Why is this? That which the Tathāgata calls "endowment with all marks" is itself a non-endowment; it is merely designated as "endowment with all marks.
One should see the Tathāgata as the pure Dharma-body, free from the characteristics of the physical body and its marks, and beyond all limitations.
The Treatise says: If the Buddha’s realm is free from both existence and non-existence, how could the physical body with its marks and signs not also be non-existent?

To dispel this doubt, it is clarified that being complete is itself non-completeness; this is intended to lead one to realize that even within the physical body and its marks and signs, [the true nature is revealed].
One realizes that there is no division and no portion, because one attains the vision of the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body.
As for this pure Dharma-body, its essence is the Dharma-realm; it is not restricted to the six-foot body or the thirty-two marks. Thus, those bodies of six feet and those marks of thirty-two—
Each and every one of these is itself an ocean of marks and embellishments; they must not be viewed merely as the sixteen-foot body with its forty-eight features.
Subhūti, you should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall preach some Dharma. Do not have such a thought. Why?
If anyone says that the Tathāgata has preached some Dharma, they slander the Buddha; they do not understand.
Subhūti, it is because of what I have said: "One who preaches the Dharma does not preach any dharma; this is called preaching the Dharma. To explain:
since the nature of that which is preached is unpreachable and inherently detached, one avoids the charge of sophistry by understanding that preaching is non-preaching.
[Objection: If the marks and signs of the physical body (rūpakāya) are not fully perfected, how could there be no verbal component when preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings?
[Is this] a medicine? How can sentient beings, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s discourse, understand the various vehicles?
To dispel this doubt, it is said: "If one says that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, that person slanders the Buddha, for they are unable to understand what I have taught.
What I have taught is such that not even the slightest characteristic of a dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is to be found; there is nothing taught."
Characteristics. There is no one able to describe characteristics, because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of sounds and syllables;

and because the nature of all sounds and syllables is not sound or syllable, it is precisely the dharma of non-nature. Within this, there is not even a single word that can be spoken. This fully negates two types of false views (*apavāda*):
first, to negate the false view that there is a dharma that can be spoken of; second, to negate the total denial of speaking any dharma at all.
Because of slandering it—meaning that what is spoken is not spoken; it is not by remaining silent that one is said to have no speech.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who..."
"Upon hearing this Dharma, will they give rise to faith? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
Why is this? Subhūti, as for 'sentient beings,' the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings; it is merely a designation called 'sentient beings.'"
This Dharma is difficult to believe, yet there are those who do believe it; for all sentient beings are not [truly] born. The commentary states:
This is a further doubt regarding the difficulty of accepting it through faith. However, sentient beings are fundamentally not substantially existent by nature as sentient beings.

It is only due to a single moment of delusion that they are conventionally designated as "sentient beings. When one attains awakening in a single thought-moment, their very substance is itself the Buddha.
Both Buddhas and sentient beings are established through conventional truth and verbal expression, yet ultimately they possess no real intrinsic nature.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when a Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Regarding my *anuttara*..."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. There is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because it is without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span, one cultivates the one...
All wholesome dharmas lead immediately to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas.
Subhūti, if there were someone who took all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm, and likewise gathered heaps of the seven treasures...
If someone were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, their merit would surpass that of the former;
the latter would not equal a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor ten-thousandth, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor a billionth part of it.
It is even beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Wisdom is the equality of non-apprehension of phenomena; wholesome and unwholesome dharmas together constitute Bodhi.
From the total nature arises cultivation, and cultivation is itself the nature. Therefore, the merit of upholding and explaining this is vast.

The Treatise says: If, in the ultimate sense, the realm of the Buddha cannot be apprehended through either physical characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) or verbal expression, how could it be otherwise for the essential nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) of the Dharma-body? To dispel this doubt, it is said:
"In my unsurpassed enlightenment, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended. This is because this dharma is equal, being without high or low. Please provide some proof of this.
As for "all dharmas," they are simply the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Regarding "form having no high or low": it is like a single river of the Ganges;
fish and dragons regard it as their dwelling place, asuras regard it as weapons and staves, while humans regard it as clear spring water.
Hungry ghosts perceive it as pus and blood; those of the Two Vehicles realize its fundamental emptiness; Bodhisattvas know its various distinctions;
and with the Buddha-eye, one knows it to be the Dharma-realm. Yet the nature of the water in the Ganges has no high or low; it is only that the deluded perceptions of sentient beings differ.
One should know that all forms are likewise so. As for sound having no high or low, it is, for example:
A single incantation: when Māras and heretics hear it, they are terrified; when the sons of the Buddha hear it, they find peace and security.

It is like when Māra used harsh sounds to frighten the Buddha, yet they were instead transformed into hymns of praise. When the Northern Court suffered defeat, the mere sound of the wind or the cry of a crane was taken by all to be the army of the Jin.
One should know that all sounds are likewise thus. As for fragrance having no high or low, it is like, for example, in the world...

Regarding the absence of superiority or inferiority in odor: when the scent of aloeswood and sandalwood reaches flies and gnats, they depart from afar. When the Buddha sits in the latrine of a phantom monk, it immediately becomes a fragrant palace.
Regarding the absence of superiority or inferiority in taste: for example, when Maudgalyāyana’s alms-food was touched by his mother, it turned into burning coals;
yet in an age of famine, when the Buddha received horse-barley, it became like nectar. Regarding the absence of superiority or inferiority in touch: for example, as in the midst of darkness...

He touches his knee. Fearing that it might belong to another, the dragon rains down swords and staves, which transform into celestial flowers and the like. There is no high or low among all phenomena (*dharmas*).
For example, generating the bodhicitta for the sake of fame and profit is a cause for the three miserable realms;
whereas, for the sake of severing the evil killing of a Brahmin, one’s merit increases all the more. Therefore, the nature of all phenomena is equal; they are fundamentally non-existent.
High and low: according to the deluded perceptions of sentient beings' minds, there appear high and low; yet these high and low are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
To realize this absence of intrinsic nature is called unsurpassed *bodhi*; it is not that some separate, minor dharma can be attained.
Having thus demonstrated that *bodhi* is non-attainable, he then precisely indicates the essential method for sublime cultivation, saying: "By means of no-self and no-person..."
Without [the notion of] sentient beings or a life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas and thereby attains unsurpassed bodhi.
Failing to realize selflessness while cultivating all wholesome dharmas merely results in the false fruits of humans and devas.

Cultivating no wholesome dharmas while merely realizing the emptiness of the self merely results in the small fruits of the two vehicles. To falsely claim that both self and dharmas are empty [in such cases] is a delusion.
Yet, if one acts wantonly according to evil dharmas, one becomes a seed of the icchantika hell.
Only by cultivating all virtues through non-self can one truly abide in what is called "giving rise to the mind without dwelling on anything. Thus, one immediately attains unsurpassed bodhi.
Now, this Dharma is equal and without high or low; this is the excellence of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It is devoid of self, person, sentient being, or life-span;
this is the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna*). One cultivates all wholesome dharmas; this is the excellence of practice (*caryā*). When these three factors constitute the vehicle, one attains Bodhi.
Furthermore, the statement that "wholesome dharmas are not wholesome dharmas" and so forth is for the purpose of dispelling doubt, lest [one should] fear...
A doubt arises: "If not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, how can one further cultivate all wholesome dharmas?

Are these wholesome dharmas not, in fact, merely non-dharmas? To resolve this, it is said: Wholesome dharmas are themselves non-wholesome dharmas. This is because "wholesome" is a name applied in contrast to "unwholesome.
It is only in dependence upon unwholesome dharmas that wholesome dharmas are provisionally designated. If there were no opposition to the unwholesome, the name "wholesome" would not exist.
Therefore, all wholesome dharmas are cultivated solely by the mind; since the mind itself does not exist, these wholesome dharmas are also empty of intrinsic nature, for they cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, all wholesome dharmas mutually encompass all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, because their nature is not fixed.

For example, although practices such as giving and observing the precepts are wholesome dharmas, if one cultivates them with a mind that seeks fame, profit, or artificial adornment, this is [the third...]
Cultivating with a mind of competitiveness between self and others is the cause for asuras. Cultivating with a mind attached to signs and calculating for results is the cause for humans and devas.
Cultivating with a mind seeking to extinguish suffering and transcend the world is the cause for the two vehicles.
Cultivating with a mind to benefit sentient beings is the cause for bodhisattvas. Cultivating with a mind of the equality of the dharma-realm is the cause for the Unsurpassed [Way].
Such distinctions are immeasurable. Because all wholesome dharmas are in essence the Dharma-realm, their true mark is signless and inconceivable.
Thus, the concluding statement, "these are called wholesome dharmas," is made in contrast to unwholesome causes and conditions.

Because the mind alone is empty and quiescent; because it gives rise to the ten realms; and because it is the entire substance of the Dharma-realm—such wholesome dharmas arise entirely from the nature (xing).
Therefore, they are called "cultivation" (xiu). Since cultivation itself is the nature, there are no substantial dharmas.
This is the most perfect and the most sudden; it is the ultimate meaning among all ultimate meanings. How could the merit of upholding and expounding this ever be compared to that of material giving?
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? Because, in reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata says that there is a self, it is not a self; yet ordinary people imagine that there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called ordinary persons by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary persons; they are merely designated as "ordinary persons.
Knowing that birth is non-birth, one thus crosses over [to the other shore]. The teaching of self and no-self is likewise so:
both the ordinary person and the extraordinary person are empty by their very nature. Therefore, all provisional designations are indestructible.
The Treatise says: Previously it was explained that sentient beings are in fact not sentient beings.
How then can there be a sūtra stating, "Immeasurable sentient beings take the Buddha as their spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and are liberated from all suffering"? To dispel this doubt, it is said:

"In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. This is because, within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), both the Buddha and sentient beings lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
Because of great compassion based on the identity of essence, there are no sentient beings existing apart from the mind.
If there were truly sentient beings distinct from the Tathāgata who were the objects of his deliverance, then the Tathāgata would possess the four marks such as a self.

It should be understood that although the Tathāgata occasionally speaks of a "self," this is merely a provisional designation; in reality, there is no self. Yet, when ordinary people hear these words...

This arises from giving rise to views and generating attachment on one's own part. Furthermore, fearing that one might further calculate that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is a substantially real phenomenon (*dravyasat*), he explains accordingly:
"They are not ordinary persons," because both the noble (*ārya*) and the ordinary are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), having never possessed a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the statement "this is called an ordinary person," it is merely that their conventional designations have not been destroyed.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti said, "So it is, so it is; the Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if [one were to perceive him] by means of..."
Regarding those who perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks: a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) is himself a Tathāgata. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, this person..."
Those who walk in false paths cannot see the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of marks; this should be understood as the removal of attachment.
Regarding the discourse on being free from the four propositions, it has already been elucidated repeatedly that all marks are non-marks. Now, this question is again posed.

This is because he intends to fully eliminate all conceptual phrases. He does not say "seeing the Tathāgata," but rather says "contemplating the Tathāgata," because the Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*). If so, would the thirty-two marks alone not be among all phenomena?
Would they alone lack the meaning of suchness that can be contemplated? Therefore, Subhūti replied in accordance with this: "So it is, so it is. Because...
One contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. However, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is ultimately beyond the four propositions.
If one were to contemplate [the Buddha] solely by means of the thirty-two marks, then even a Wheel-turning Sage King could be considered a Tathāgata.
How could one know the Tathāgata’s Dharma-nature body? The Venerable One understood the meaning but was unable to respond immediately.
The Buddha then completed the teaching with a verse: "To seek it only by means of form and sound is certainly a deviant path;
to seek it apart from form and sound is likewise a deviant path. To seek it both as identical to and apart from them is neither identical nor apart."
These are all heterodox paths. According to the original treatises, each contains two verses; the first verse is the same [as yours], while the second verse says:
"The Tathāgata takes the Dharma as his body; one should contemplate only the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). The nature of phenomena is not an object of vision, and thus it cannot be known.
In this way, both the text and the meaning are complete.
Subhūti, if you should have this thought: "The Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of perfection," Subhūti, do not have this thought.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of perfection. Subhūti, if you should have this thought: "Having set forth..."
Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, do not entertain the thought that it teaches the annihilation of all phenomena.
Why is this? One who has resolved upon the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
The four propositions are all free from [marks]; the marks and signs are perfect.

Regarding the statement, "From the initial resolve, one never speaks of a doctrine of annihilation": if the Tathāgata cannot be sought through form or sound, and even the four propositions are unattainable.
"Could it be that there is a characteristic of ultimate annihilation? To dispel this doubt, it is said, "Do not conceive such thoughts," and so forth.
One must understand that because the Tathāgata is free from the four extremes, he is fully endowed with infinite marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
If he were merely like a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), then after casting off his body, his marks and signs would perish, and he would instead become... [the opposite].
This is the mark of annihilation,
Subhūti. If a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in charity,
yet another person were to know that all phenomena are without self and attain patient endurance (*kṣānti*), this latter bodhisattva would surpass the former.
The merit obtained by the Bodhisattva—why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva does not accept merit?
Subhūti, regarding the merit performed by a bodhisattva, one should not be greedily attached to it; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.
The patience regarding the ultimate truth is thereby accomplished; being without attachment and without craving, its merit is supreme.
The treatise says: By knowing that phenomena have no self, one accomplishes patience; this is the fulfillment of the power of prajñā.
Because one is neither greedy nor attached, one’s merit and virtue are beyond compare. If there were anything received, there would be a limit or measure.
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes, goes, sits, or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata neither goes nor comes, for the fruit of his virtues is ultimately unarisen.

The commentary states: If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), no merit can be grasped, why do other sūtras speak in this way, saying that the Tathāgata, having perfected the accumulations of merit and wisdom, sits upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and proceeds toward nirvāṇa? It is in order to dispel such doubts.
Therefore, it is said that such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
This is because True Suchness has no distinct location from which one could come, and birth-and-death has no distinct location to which one could go.

When conditions arise, it manifests—just as when water is clear, the moon appears, yet the moon itself does not actually come. When conditions cease, it becomes hidden—just as when water is turbid, the moon disappears.
Because the moon does not actually go away, Subhūti.
Suppose a good man or a good woman were to grind the trichiliocosm into fine dust.
What do you think? Would that mass of dust be very much? "It would be very much, World-Honored One. Why is that?
If this multitude of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called it a "multitude of atoms. Why is that?
The Buddha’s teaching of a "multitude of atoms" is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a "multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One, the trichiliocosm spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a world; it is merely designated as a "world. Why is that? If the world...
That which is a real entity as a realm is a unified whole (*piṇḍa-grāha*). The Tathāgata has said that a unified whole is not a unified whole;
it is merely called a unified whole. Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is ineffable;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.
The atom-like worlds are neither existent nor non-existent; They are neither shatterable nor unshatterable, neither conjoined nor unconjoined.
The fruit and virtue of the Tathāgata are ineffable; No analogy whatsoever can serve as a metaphor for them. The commentary states:
The above clarifies that the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; yet, when there are conditions, he appears.
Manifest when conditions arise and hidden when conditions end.

Fearing that there may be doubt—such as thinking that the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like the world-system and his *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* are like motes of dust—and further fearing doubt—such as thinking that delusion regarding *nirvāṇa* results in *saṃsāra*, like breaking the world-system into dust, while awakening regarding *saṃsāra* results in *nirvāṇa*, like joining the dust back into the world-system—the present commentary explains: "Motes..."
Dust is not dust; worlds are not worlds; even a unified mass is not a unified mass, and so forth.
This is because the Dharmakāya’s manifestations are fundamentally incomparable to worlds or atoms.
Birth-and-death and Nirvāṇa likewise cannot be illustrated by means of shattered dust or unified realms. Yet, these very atoms are not atoms. Thus it is said:
This world is, in fact, not a world; it cannot be broken, for there is nothing to break, nor can it be joined, for there is nothing to join.
It is merely that ordinary people give rise to false attachments.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, Subhūti...
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? “No, World-Honored One. This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has said.

Why is that? World-Honored One, what the Tathāgata calls the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, is itself not a view of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span;
it is merely designated as the ‘view of a self,’ the ‘view of a person.’”
The view of sentient beings and the view of a life-principle:
the wise should know that these four views are abandoned. Regarding the discourse on explaining existence and non-existence to understand the true meaning, it says:
"This section clarifies that the four views are fundamentally abandoned, serving as the skillful means for practicing Prajñā."
One might fear that there could be doubt, saying: "The Buddha refutes the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span because they exist.

If, from the beginning, there were no such things as self, person, sentient being, or life-span, what would be the use of refuting them? It is like a person who is not ill; why would they need medicine?

Now it is clarified that these four views are themselves not four views, and for this reason they can be refuted. It is like an illness that is not a real illness, and for this reason it can be cured.
The physician [removes] the cataract, which is not a substantial entity and can therefore be excised. It is simply that one must realize that the four views are fundamentally not four views.
This is like realizing that an illness is not real; then one can settle the mind and apply the treatment. The Main Section (Zhengzongfen) concludes.

Subhūti, one who has set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should know all dharmas in this way, see them in this way, and resolve with faith in this way, such that they do not give rise to the mark of dharmas (dharma-nimitta).
Subhūti, as for what is called the "mark of dharmas," the Tathāgata says it is not a mark of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "mark of dharmas."
"Thus, through knowledge, vision, and resolute belief, because the characteristics of phenomena are non-characteristics, they do not arise.
The commentary states: This is the entrustment for circulation. "Thus" refers broadly to what was explained in the preceding text.

"Knowledge and vision" refers to the time of realization; "resolute belief" refers to the time of cultivation and study. During the actual time of cultivation and study, the characteristics of phenomena do not arise.
Because the characteristic of dharmas is itself the non-characteristic of dharmas. It is merely in accordance with conventional truth that they are called "characteristics of dharmas.

Subhūti, if someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and upholds this sutra—even for a moment...
To receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain even as little as four lines of verse for others, the merit thereof surpasses that [of the former].
The merit of giving away treasures throughout immeasurable worlds is not equal to the excellence of generating the resolve and upholding this teaching.
The commentary states: This is a comparison regarding its circulation. It is already a great difficulty to generate the bodhicitta; to uphold and explain this [teaching] is even more so.
This sutra is doubly rare. Indeed, those who have not resolved to attain bodhicitta are incapable of upholding and expounding this sutra;
yet, even for those who have resolved their minds, it cannot be perfected without upholding and expounding this sutra.

Now, because one has both resolved the mind and upheld and expounded it, its merit far exceeds that which can be reached by the blessings of ordinary giving. As the *Puṇyapradāna-śāstra* asks: "For what reason is it further said..."
Regarding the merit of upholding this: it is because one wishes to cause sentient beings to attain ultimate faith.
How should one expound it for others? Without grasping at signs, one remains as suchness, unmoving. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way.
Expounding according to the principle without grasping at signs, because one observes the essential nature and characteristics of conditioned phenomena;
thus, through these six or ninety metaphors, the nature itself is non-abiding Great Nirvāṇa.
The treatise says: This is the method for its circulation. Those who wish to propagate this sutra must not grasp at [signs].
