Regarding its characteristics: it is like *tathatā* (suchness), for it is eternally immovable. To say it is "immovable" means that it is immovable with respect to the dichotomy of emptiness and existence.
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all phenomena are entirely empty; from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all things exist.
Since the ten realms are all empty, this is not a partial or one-sided emptiness. This very emptiness is endowed with all phenomena; thus it is named [the Middle Way].

It is *tathatā* (suchness). Since it exists within all ten realms, it is not something that exists only partially. This very existence is the sublation of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and it is also called *tathatā*.
Now, because the wisdom of suchness accords with the principle of suchness, one does not grasp at the mark of partial existence, nor does one grasp at the mark of partial emptiness;
yet, phenomena such as emptiness and existence are all found to be immovable. Furthermore, when correctly expounding [the Dharma], one is not entangled [by them].

The single character’s radical: because the characteristic of words is itself the characteristic of liberation, one does not grasp at the characteristic of verbal exposition, nor does one depart from words to separately grasp the characteristic of silence.
Regarding the section beginning with "For what reason," it again demonstrates the gate of Prajñā contemplation.
"All conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) refers to the objects of observation, specifically pointing to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Vertically...
It exhausts the ten realms and extends horizontally across both matter and mind. To state it briefly:

all various provisional and substantial lands are collectively termed "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), because they are formed in accordance with defiled or pure conditions. The phrase "like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows," and so forth, indicates the gate of contemplation.
This translation contains only six metaphors, whereas other translations contain nine: namely, stars, cataracts, lamps, illusions, dew, bubbles, [shadows, reflections, and floating clouds].

Dream, lightning, and clouds—these are the ten similes from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, namely: illusion, a mirage, the moon in water, empty space, an echo, a city of the gandharvas, a dream, a shadow, a reflection in a mirror, and a magical transformation.

Although these enumerations of dharmas differ, their underlying principle is one and the same. Here, I shall provide three brief explanations: first, the explanation by way of attachment to phenomena;
second, the sequential explanation; and third, the explanation of perfect interfusion. Regarding the explanation by way of attachment to phenomena: "dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows... is...

The contemplation of non-self. The contemplation of impermanence is that [all things] are like dew and like lightning. The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is like a dream, for it cannot be found upon waking.

Sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are like illusions, for they manifest in accordance with the mind. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is like bubbles, for they arise and perish in falsehood.
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like a shadow, for it possesses no real nature. Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are like dew, for they do not endure for long. Mind...
Dharmas are like lightning, for they arise and immediately perish. Second, regarding the sequential explanation:

just as dreams and the like exist falsely due to causes and conditions, so too are all conditioned phenomena; they exist falsely due to causes and conditions and lack any substantial intrinsic nature.
Just as dreams and the like are empty in their very essence, so too are all conditioned phenomena; they are empty in their very essence. It is not...
Because they cease, they are empty. Just as dreams and other such things manifest in various ways, so too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*);

they manifest in various ways and are designated by infinite provisional names. For example, a dream is not different from sleep; an illusion is not different from its source; a bubble is not different from water;
a reflection is not different from its substance; dew is not different from moisture; and lightning is not different from light. All conditioned phenomena are likewise.
It is likewise so; it does not differ from the true nature (*dharmatā*). Regarding the "threefold perfect fusion" interpretation:

this refers to the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) within the one mind. Because one contemplates while in cessation, all things are like dreams and illusions.

Because one ceases while in contemplation, all dreams and the like are entirely suchness (*tathatā*). Through the power of this perfect cessation and contemplation within the one mind, one then knows all things.
All dharmas are, in their very nature, the great nirvāṇa of non-abiding; it is based on this that [this teaching] is expounded, and it is precisely this Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and [upāsikās], [were filled with joy].
Upāsikā. All those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
"Because the three things are pure, there is joy; the two benefits are fully realized, and one undertakes the practice.
The commentary says: This describes the characteristics of its circulation. First, the purity of the speaker:
because the Buddha has realized the essence of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, he is far removed from faults such as fame and profit. Second, the purity of the Dharma taught: it is unsurpassed.

Because it is the seal of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the True Dharma, it is free from all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) such as existence and non-existence. Third, the listener attains pure understanding;
by upholding the precepts, cultivating merit, and possessing right wisdom, they do not startle, fear, or tremble, because they are able to have deep faith.
No longer grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) or non-phenomena (*adharma*), they achieve self-benefit; this is called "faithful acceptance" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). It transforms and... [without limit].
"To exhaust" means to practice and uphold.
The inconceivable true mark of Prajñā—such a wondrous meaning is like a great ocean;
by reverently receiving the supreme power of the Triple Gem, I shall expound hereon a single drop of its characteristics.
It pierces the cataracts of the "blind from birth" who hold views of emptiness, Causing them to see the true mark as adamantine.
May this merit be bestowed upon all living beings, So that together they may achieve the ultimate perfection (pāramitā).
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: A Treatise Refuting Views of Emptiness* (End).
